sens: Royal city of Canaan in the lowlands of Judah
H5700G.detail: Eglon is a fortified city of Canaan, ruled by a king, located in the lowlands (the Shephelah) of southern Palestine. It opposed the conquest of Israel under Joshua: its king allied with four other Amorite kings to attack the Gibeonites, allies of Israel (Joshua 10:3-5). After this defeat, Joshua conquered the city itself, striking it with the sword and devoting all its inhabitants to destruction, as he had done elsewhere (Joshua 10:34-37).
H5700G.origine: The name Eglon literally means "calf-like" or "bovine" in Hebrew, an image perhaps evoking the fertility or strength of this agricultural region. It is a specific geographical location in Canaan, mentioned during the conquest and whose importance lay in its strategic position in the lowlands of southern Judah.
H5700G.emploi: Eglon appears eight times in the Bible, all in the book of Joshua, in chapter 10 (the great battle against the five Amorite kings) and in chapters 12 and 15 (geographical lists). The city is always presented in a context of conflict with Israel: it represents the resistance of the land of Canaan to the possession promised by God. Its king, specifically mentioned, participated in the coalition that sought to annihilate Israel, before Joshua conquered the city and placed it under divine ban.

sens: King of Moab who oppressed Israel
Corpulent and cruel man
H5700H.detail:
1. Eglon is the king of the kingdom of Moab who, during the time of the Judges, dominated the people of Israel for eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14). The Lord had strengthened him against Israel as punishment for Israel's unfaithfulness. This oppression lasted until Ehud, a judge raised up by God, killed him by delivering a secret message in the palace (Judges 3:15-17).
2. The text also emphasizes that Eglon was "a very fat man" (Judges 3:17), a detail that contrasts with the cunning of Ehud and perhaps symbolizes an arrogant and carnal power, quickly brought down by God's judge.
H5700H.origine: The name Eglon means "young calf" or "calf," formed from the Hebrew root designating the calf, an animal associated with physical strength. This name evokes the image of a powerful but unwise creature, fitting for an oppressive king whose reign God would end.
H5700H.emploi: Eglon appears only in the account of Judges 3, where he is presented as the king of Moab who oppressed Israel for eighteen years. Israel, having apostatized, was delivered to this oppression; the children of Israel "cried out to the Lord" (Judges 3:15), who raised up Ehud to deliver them. The text describes him as a corpulent man, a detail that underscores his comfort and satisfaction in his oppression, contrasting with the swiftness of his death at the hands of the judge.
H5700H.portee: The story of Eglon teaches that no oppression escapes God: even a powerful king who subjugates God's people cannot long resist His justice. It also shows that deliverance comes from God alone, who raises up unexpected deliverers like Ehud to break the chains and restore His people.

sens: to be moved with compassion in the face of another's suffering
to feel sorrow at misfortune
H5701.detail:
1. To have pity means to be touched at heart by the distress of another person. It is a motion of tenderness and sympathy towards one who suffers. In Job 30:25, the man states that he had tears for the unfortunate and that his heart felt pity for the needy: he speaks of this natural ability to empathize with the misfortune of others.
2. The word also expresses inner pain, that affliction of the heart caused by witnessing great misery. It is less an action than a disposition of the heart, a feeling that grips one who contemplates suffering.
H5701.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of being touched, being emotionally affected. It is a movement of the heart rather than an external action. The form used here (Qal) is the simple and direct form: the feeling exists and is naturally experienced.
H5701.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 30:25. Job defends himself against his accusers by recalling that he has always had a merciful heart: he has wept over the misfortune of others and his soul has been moved by the poverty of the needy. It is a testimony to his moral righteousness and natural compassion, at a time when he himself is undergoing the worst suffering.
H5701.portee: This word reminds us that the ability to suffer with those who suffer is a mark of righteousness and piety. For the Christian, having pity is not a weakness: it is a manifestation of the heart of God Himself, who suffers with His creatures and intervenes to save them. It is a call to cultivate compassion towards the unfortunate.

sens: to confine oneself, to shut oneself in
to hold back one's words, to remain silent
to isolate oneself, to stay apart
H5702.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of closing oneself off, voluntarily shutting oneself in: the one who acts withdraws, closing off from the outside like behind a barrier. 2. In the realm of words, it means to hold back what one might say, to remain silent — not out of forced mutism, but by voluntary reserve. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi shuts herself up in her sorrow and does not want her daughters-in-law to hope in her: she refrains from promising them a future that she believes is impossible. 3. By extension, the word evokes emotional isolation: shutting oneself in, refusing communion or exchange, staying apart.
H5702.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of barrier, enclosure, limitation. It belongs to the family of verbs that express spatial or moral confinement: something that holds back, that closes. The context of Ruth 1:13 in ancient Israel shows the usage in a situation where the heart closes under the weight of grief and despair.
H5702.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ruth 1:13. Naomi uses it to tell her daughters-in-law that she cannot give them hope: "Would you wait until they grow up? Would you tie yourselves to them, and would you give up marrying? No, my daughters: for I am very bitter, and the hand of the Lord has been heavy upon me." The word expresses her refusal to maintain hope, her withdrawal into herself in mourning.
H5702.portee: This word shows how grief and suffering can close us off from ourselves. For the believer, it invites recognition of when pain becomes isolation — and to seek instead openness to God and fellowship, as Naomi herself will discover with Ruth.

sens: What lasts without end, which will never stop
What comes from the most ancient past
What belongs to divine eternity
H5703.detail:
1. The word expresses what continues without interruption, without limit in time — an infinite duration that will have no end. This is what the psalmist means when he cries: "I will extol you, my God, O King! And I will bless your name forever and ever" (Psalms 145:1): his praise will never have an end. Or again: "The Lord will reign forever and ever" (Exodus 15:18) — his reign will have no end.
2. The word can also designate what belongs to the past, the ancient, what dates back to the origins. This is rarer in the provided usages, but it is a meaning of the word in Hebrew.
3. Applied to God, the word takes on its full force: it speaks of divine eternity, this timeless existence of the Creator that does not change and will never end. "The Lord, the Lord is the rock of ages" (Isaiah 26:4): this eternal rock on which one can lean at any time.
H5703.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of advancing, continuing, of "not stopping." It has given in Hebrew several words of the same family that speak of duration and continuity. In French, it is often rendered by "forever," "eternally," "for always," or "perpetuity," depending on the context and the desired effect.
H5703.emploi: This word appears 47 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Psalms (more than 25 occurrences) and the prophets (Isaiah, Daniel, etc.). It primarily expresses the permanence of God's work: his reign (Exodus 15:18), his justice (Psalms 9:6), his faithfulness (Psalms 111:8). It also describes the duration of the blessing granted to the righteous: "The righteous shall inherit the earth, and dwell therein forever" (Psalms 37:29). It is finally used for the eternity of God himself: "The Lord endures forever" (Psalms 9:6, Psalms 10:16). Note: sometimes "never" (negative translation) renders the same word when it concerns what will never cease to not be.
H5703.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not subject to time as we are: his reign, his promises, his goodness will never wear out. It invites a limitless trust in the Lord, for what comes from him lasts forever. It is a call to consider our lives in the light of God's eternity, and not the concerns of the moment.

sens: Mark the endpoint or spatial limit of a movement, an extent
Mark the endpoint or temporal limit of a duration, an event
Indicate a degree, an intensity reached
Serve as a conjunction to express purpose or consequence
H5704.detail:
1. This preposition indicates where something stops or extends in space. In Genesis 10:19, it delineates the territory of the Canaanites: "until Sodom." It also marks the place where a movement ends, as in Numbers 13:23 where the Israelites arrive "until the valley of Eshcol."
2. It marks when an action stops or continues in time. In Genesis 3:19, God says to Adam: "until you return to the ground" — the limiting moment when his life ceases. In 1 Kings 8:8, the bars of the ark have been there "until this day," indicating a continuity up to the moment of the narrative.
3. It expresses an extreme degree, a limit of intensity. In Isaiah 37:3, the children are "near to breaking out" marking a critical situation. It can translate an equality of condition: "even until" means "even as."
4. In combination with other words, it takes on the value of a conjunction to indicate purpose or consequence: "until" introduces a condition or an expected result.
H5704.origine: The Hebrew word עַד (ad) is a very ancient primary preposition, probably related to the idea of "walking towards" or "reaching." It also exists in Aramaic with the same meaning. It is one of the most common grammatical tools in the biblical text, used over a thousand times in Genesis alone. Its fundamental meaning is spatial (to go that far), from which it naturally extends to time (to persist until then) and to degree (to go to that point).
H5704.emploi: This preposition appears about 1127 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly abundant in the narratives of Genesis and Exodus. It marks territorial boundaries (Genesis 10:19: "until Sodom"), the stages of a journey (Numbers 13:23), and the limiting moments of an action (Genesis 3:19: "until you return"). Often combined with other prepositions like "from...until" (with min), it frames a complete extent or duration. Its use gradually extends from the concrete (a territorial limit) to the abstract (a limit of time or intensity), passing through values of temporal or final conjunctions ("until"). It is a key word for expressing movement, duration, and purpose in the biblical narrative.
H5704.portee: Understanding this word shows how the Bible situates human action in space and time, always marked by limits and boundaries. For the believer, "until" reminds us that God sets boundaries to our history: a promised land (Genesis until), a lifespan ("until you return to the dust"), a moment of judgment. It is also a word of hope: God accompanies his people "until" the end (Genesis 28:15). This word woven throughout Scripture reveals that our life is neither infinite nor directionless — it is marked by divine purpose.

sens: Until the moment when, during the entire period preceding
Towards, to a limit point in space or time
Marks a temporal limit: before a certain date or event
Introduces a condition or duration: as long as, for as long as
H5705.detail:
1. This word primarily expresses the idea of continuity in time: an action or state persists until the moment when something changes. For example, King Darius "until sunset" tried to save Daniel (Daniel 6:14), meaning he persevered during that entire duration.

2. It can also mark a precise spatial or temporal limit towards which one is heading or extending. When it is said that Nebuchadnezzar's body was "until his hair grew like eagle's feathers" (Daniel 4:33), it describes the prolongation of a situation until a point of culmination.

3. Often, the word introduces a deadline or a limit date before which something cannot happen. Ezra orders that the city of Jerusalem shall not be rebuilt "before" an authorization from the king (Ezra 4:21), thus marking the moment from which the action becomes permitted.

4. In the passages of the prophecies of Daniel, it often structures long descriptions where what persists is enumerated "until" a decisive turning point or judgment (Daniel 7:11: the beast "was destroyed"), thus delimiting the duration of a temporal reality.
H5705.origine: This Hebrew-Aramaic word is a fundamental preposition and conjunction used to mark time and space. The root evokes the idea of "reaching" or "attaining," hence its use to designate a limit point that one approaches or reaches. It belongs to the family of words expressing limit, boundary, the end of an extension. In biblical Aramaic (notably in Daniel and Ezra), this word plays the same role as the Hebrew preposition "ad" of the Old Testament.
H5705.emploi: This word appears 31 times in the provided texts, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which are in Aramaic. It functions as a preposition (introducing a noun or noun group) and as a conjunction (introducing a clause). In Ezra, it marks administrative and religious deadlines (before the king's authorization, before the completion of the Temple). In Daniel, it structures prophetic visions by delineating periods: the reigns of the beasts persist "until" divine judgment, the sufferings of Nebuchadnezzar last "until" his deliverance. This word is rarely translated unambiguously in French; depending on the context, it becomes "until," "before," "during," or phrases like "in the end."
H5705.portee: This word helps the reader grasp God's plan in history. It reminds us that every period, every reign, every trial has a limit set by God himself: nothing is eternal except his word. For the believer facing difficulty, this word is a promise: there is always a "until" beyond which things change and where divine justice or grace intervenes.

sens: What a carnivorous animal catches and devours
What is taken from a defeated enemy: the spoils of war
Figuratively: one who is defenseless and delivered to the domination of another
H5706.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of an animal hunting: the prey it seizes and eats. In Genesis 49:27, Benjamin is compared to "a wolf that tears" — in the morning he "devours the prey," in the evening he "divides the spoils," an image of a voracious and victorious beast.
2. By extension, it designates the spoils taken from a defeated enemy. In Isaiah 33:23, after the fall of a great army, "the spoils of an immense booty are shared" — it is the fruit of victory, what the victors take from the enemy.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to one who is defenseless against a stronger predator, delivered to its mercy like game with no escape.
H5706.origine: The Hebrew word עַד (ad) comes from a root that evokes the idea of taking, seizing. It belongs to the family of words related to capture and spoils. The basic image is that of the hunter catching his prey or the warrior seizing the spoils of his adversary — an image of brute force and dispossession.
H5706.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 49:27, Jacob prophesies about Benjamin by comparing him to a wolf: it is an image of warrior power and ferocity — Benjamin will devour the prey like a carnivore. In Isaiah 33:23, the context is that of the fall of a great enemy: its spoils become common prey, and even the weakest ("the lame") partake. In both cases, the word evokes complete domination and overwhelming victory.
H5706.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the reality of spiritual conflict: it serves to describe those who, without God's protection, would become easy prey for evil and injustice. It highlights our natural vulnerability and the importance of Christ's victory, who has rescued us from the power of darkness (Colossians 1:13) and makes us victors rather than victims.

sens: a person who has seen or heard something and can report on it
material proof or visible sign that attests to a fact
what is said to confirm the truthfulness of an action or word
a person or thing established to serve as a guarantor of a commitment
one who attests to the truth of another or a cause
one who bears witness to God or divine truth
H5707.detail:
1. The witness is primarily one who has witnessed an event and can speak about it: they have seen or heard with their own ears. In trials, the Bible requires at least two concordant witnesses to establish a serious fact (Deuteronomy 19:15), and false witnessing is a severe crime (Deuteronomy 5:20).
2. The word also designates the proof itself, what attests to a fact: an object, a sign, a stone erected to memorialize a covenant. The altar built by the tribes of Transjordan becomes a visible "witness" of their union with Israel (Joshua 22:28).
3. To testify is to affirm what one has seen to establish the truth. A sincere witness speaks rightly; a lying witness destroys (Proverbs 21:28).
4. A witness can also be a person or thing that is constituted as a guarantor: a monument is erected as a testimony of a promise (Genesis 31:44), so that everyone remembers their commitment.
5. In the early books of Isaiah, the word takes on a spiritual significance: God establishes the servant, then Israel as a "witness" to the nations, that is, as one who proclaims the truth of God (Isaiah 43:10).
H5707.origine: The Hebrew word עֵד comes from a root that means "to be present, to witness." A witness is therefore literally "one who is there," who was present at the time of the events. The notion of presence is at the heart of the word: to be a witness is to have seen with one's own eyes or heard with one's own ears, to be a direct observer. This root also exists in Arabic and Aramaic with the same meaning.
H5707.emploi: The word appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the legislative books (Torah) and in biblical wisdom (Proverbs, Job). In the Torah, it is a major legal term: Moses regulates judicial procedure, insisting on the number of witnesses necessary for a conviction (Deuteronomy 17:6, 19:15) and punishing false testimony severely (Exodus 20:16). In Proverbs, the theme of the faithful or lying witness often recurs, as biblical wisdom links justice to the truth of the word. Isaiah uses it in a new way: Israel and the servant of God become "witnesses" of his divinity and salvation to the nations (Isaiah 43:10, 44:8). The word thus encompasses three areas: the legal, the wisdom, and the prophetic.
H5707.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of truth and integrity. To be a witness is a sacred responsibility: to say what one has truly seen, not to lie to benefit a friend or harm an enemy. For the Christian, Isaiah also opens a spiritual perspective: the believer is called to be a witness to the truth of God in the world, not through a legal position but through their life and living testimony.

sens: State of what is impure, dirty, contaminated
Menstruation, state of ritual impurity
Stained and repugnant clothing or linen
Moral and spiritual condition of guilt
H5708.detail:
1. The word first designates a physical defilement, what is dirty, impure, unworthy. It is the image of a stained, worn, repugnant garment — like that of a sick or impure person according to the Law of Moses.
2. It concretely relates to the laws of impurity in Israelite worship, particularly menstruation, which temporarily rendered someone unfit for temple service.
3. The Bible uses it figuratively to depict human guilt and sin: our best actions, our "righteousness" even, resemble a filthy garment in the eyes of God. In Isaiah 64:5, the prophet cries that all the inhabitants of Judah, even their most righteous acts, are like soiled garments of menstruation — the most repulsive image for a pious Israelite.
H5708.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "to be defiled" or "to be unfit." The noun עִדָּה (idah) originally designates menstrual impurity according to the Law, then by extension anything that renders someone or something unfit for worship or morally repugnant. This notion of ritual impurity is central in the Torah and structures the distinction between the pure and the impure.
H5708.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in Isaiah 64:5, where it is translated as "defiled." The prophet uses it in figurative and poetic language to describe the moral state of Judah: even human righteousness, even the best works, are in the eyes of the holy God like an impure garment, so deep is the guilt of the people. It is a cry of repentance and humiliation before divine holiness. The word oscillates between the concrete (menstrual and ritual impurity) and the figurative (moral sin), but it is always the image of disgust and indignity that dominates.
H5708.portee: This word powerfully reminds us of the infinite gap between God's holiness and man's sinful condition. No human effort, no righteousness of our own strength, can make us acceptable before God: we remain defiled as long as we are not purified by his forgiveness. It is a call to humility and awareness of our need for grace — a central theme of the Gospel.

sens: Go beyond, cross or exceed something
Disappear, cease to exist or be in effect
Remove, take away, take something from someone
Remain unchanged, not be touched or affected
H5709.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of movement: to pass is to cross a space, to go beyond a limit. For example, in Daniel 3:27, the smell of the fire did not "reach" the three young men: it did not cross the barrier of their protection to touch them.

2. Hence the meaning of disappearance: what passes goes away, ceases to be present. Thus in Daniel 6:8 and 6:12, the law of the Medes and Persians is "immutable" — it does not pass, does not disappear, remains stable forever.

3. The verb also means to remove or take away: to take something from someone, to snatch it away. In Daniel 4:31, the kingdom will be "taken away" from Nebuchadnezzar; in Daniel 5:20, he was "stripped" of his glory — kingship and honor were taken from him.

4. Finally, it expresses the idea of what cannot be reached or changed: to be "immutable" means that no decree can pass over you, that you cannot be surpassed or changed.
H5709.origine: The Aramaic verb עֲדָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of movement, of crossing. The P'al (simple form) means "to pass," the basic sense of crossing or exceeding. The Aphel (causative form, which makes the action active) means "to make pass" or "to remove," that is, to set something in motion out of its place or to take something away. This image of movement that crosses or removes is at the heart of the word.
H5709.emploi: This Aramaic word appears 9 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the book of Daniel. The usages are clearly divided: on one hand, the sense of removing or stripping, used for royal acts (removing the kingdom, stripping of glory); on the other hand, the sense of immutable or unchanged, applied to the laws of the Medes and Persians that cannot be revoked. In Daniel 2:21, God "changes the circumstances" — the word designates what passes, what is taken away and replaced. In Daniel 7:12, the power of the kingdoms is "taken away." This word emphasizes the omnipotence of God and kings, their ability to transform or strip away.
H5709.portee: This word reveals that nothing earthly is permanent: kingdoms pass, glory is stripped away, empires fade. For the reader, it is an invitation not to place trust in human powers, which sooner or later will be entwined by time. Only what comes from God is truly immutable and enduring.

sens: Move from one place to another, cross a space
Progress, advance in a direction
Cross, go beyond an obstacle or limit
Flow away, disappear (speaking of time or a situation)
H5710A.detail:
1. To pass means to move from one point to another, as when one crosses a path or an obstacle. In Job 28:8, the lion has never passed through the mine where wisdom lies: it has never tread upon that hidden ground. It is a physical, concrete movement.

2. The word can express the idea of advancing, progressing. It describes the act of setting out or continuing one’s path without stopping, leaving something behind.

3. To pass also means to cross a boundary, a threshold, a limit – to go beyond what was previously there. It is to cross a barrier or an obstacle that separates two states or two spaces.

4. Used figuratively, to pass evokes the flow of time or the disappearance of a situation. What passes moves away and does not return: the context of Proverbs 25:20 suggests an action that is accomplished and completed.
H5710A.origine: The verb עָדָה (adah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of movement and crossing. In Hebrew, the family of this word encompasses the idea of passing over or beyond. The Aramaic uses the same word with the same meaning: "to pass." It is a simple and ancient verb that primarily conveys physical displacement.
H5710A.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Old Testament according to available sources. In Job 28:8, in the poetic description of hidden wisdom, it expresses that the most powerful animals have never trodden the underground path where it is found: a sense of physical movement or passage. In Proverbs 25:20, the parallel context reinforces this idea of movement or transition. The verb is mainly used to describe a concrete crossing: going from one side to the other, crossing a space, leaving something behind.
H5710A.portee: This word reminds the reader that movement, passage, and progression are at the heart of life. Wisdom, as in Job 28, is found beyond where most are content to stay; it requires "passing" into deeper regions of the knowledge of God. The verb invites one not to stop, to continue the path that the Lord lays out.

sens: to adorn oneself with ornaments, to adorn
to dress someone in finery, to embellish someone
to make oneself beautiful to seduce or impress
H5710B.detail:
1. To adorn oneself literally means to dress in ornaments, jewelry, or elegant clothing to enhance one’s appearance. It is the action of someone who dresses with care. In Isaiah 61:10, the bride adorns herself with her jewels as a gesture of beauty and joy.
2. To adorn someone is to dress them in ornaments or finery — it is the action of a third party who beautifies. In Ezekiel 16:11, God adorns Jerusalem by placing bracelets on her hands and a necklace around her neck, like a master adorning his beloved.
3. To adorn oneself can also express the intention to seduce or impress through appearance. In Jeremiah 4:30, the woman adorns herself with gold ornaments and puts on eye makeup, but it is in vain because it will not save her life — the emphasis is then on the vanity of these efforts.
H5710B.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of dressing or equipping oneself. The family of the word includes nouns designating adornment, ornament, beauty accessory. The basic image is that of wrapping or covering oneself with what beautifies — which is why the same word can mean both the action of adorning oneself and that of dressing someone in finery.
H5710B.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly among the prophets. It describes either the action of adorning oneself (women, brides, Jerusalem) or that of dressing someone in ornaments. In Ezekiel 16, it paints the divine love towards Jerusalem, which is adorned like a cherished bride. In Jeremiah 4:30 and 23:40, it contrasts futile outward beauty with the coming judgment — the people adorn themselves to seduce their lovers, but in vain. In Isaiah 61:10, it expresses the joy of redemption: the soul rejoices in being adorned with the garments of salvation by God. The word thus carries a concrete meaning but often has a spiritual or symbolic significance.
H5710B.portee: This word reminds us that outward beauty is fragile and can lead to sin when it becomes pride or seduction. But it also teaches us that God cares for His people and adorns them like a bride — it is an image of tenderness and restoration. In Isaiah 61:10, being adorned with salvation by God is a reason for deep joy, far more than any earthly beauty.

sens: First wife of Lamech, antediluvian ancestor
Mother of Jabal and Jubal
H5711G.detail:
1. Ada is the first of Lamech's two wives, mentioned at the beginning of human history before the Flood (Genesis 4:19). Her name means "ornament" in Hebrew, suggesting beauty or grace. She represents one of the earliest women in the biblical genealogy.
2. Ada is the mother of Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:20). Jabal is the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock, while Jubal is the father of all who play the harp and the flute. Through her sons, Ada is the ancestor of two important lineages: the pastoral nomads and the musicians.
H5711G.origine: The name Ada comes from the Hebrew ‫עָדָה‬ (adah) and literally means "ornament" or "adornment." This name was used in the ancient Near East. The meaning of the name evokes grace or beauty, which aligns with her portrayal as Lamech's wife in the context of the generations before the Flood.
H5711G.emploi: Ada appears three times in the Bible, all in Genesis 4. She is first introduced as one of Lamech's two wives (4:19), marking an important turning point in human history: it is the first mention of polygamy in the biblical text. Then, Genesis 4:20 establishes Ada as the mother of Jabal, the founder of nomadic pastoral culture. Finally, in Genesis 4:23, she is mentioned alongside Zillah when Lamech speaks to them about his crime. Ada thus embodies the beginning of humanity before the judgment of the Flood.
H5711G.portee: Ada reminds us that the generations preceding the Flood were real human beings, with families, descendants, and cultural legacies. Her story highlights how, even in the antediluvian generations marked by increasing sin, God allowed for procreation and the development of arts and skills. She illustrates the extent of humanity's fall before divine judgment.

sens: Canaanite woman, wife of Esau
Mother of Esau's firstborn son, Eliphaz
H5711H.detail: Ada is a woman from Canaan, the daughter of Elon the Hittite, whom the patriarch Esau married. She is one of his three wives mentioned in chapter 36 of Genesis (Genesis 36:2). She is best known as the mother of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn son, of whom she is the direct ancestor: she "bore Eliphaz to Esau" (Genesis 36:4). Through Eliphaz, she also becomes the grandmother of Amalek and other sons, making her an important maternal figure in the genealogy of the people of Edom (Genesis 36:12, 36:16).
H5711H.origine: The name Ada means "ornament" in Hebrew. It is a short and clear name, typical of antediluvian and patriarchal women. Ada appears twice in the genealogy of the early humans: one Ada is mentioned as Lamech's wife (Genesis 4), long before the flood. The text clearly distinguishes this antediluvian Ada from the one we see here, Esau's wife, who lived several millennia later.
H5711H.emploi: Ada appears exactly five times in Genesis, all in chapter 36, which lists the descendants of Esau and the chiefs of Edom. Her name is mentioned each time to identify her as mother or ancestor: in Genesis 36:2, she is named among the women Esau took; in Genesis 36:4, she is presented as the mother of Eliphaz; in Genesis 36:10 and 36:12, she is recalled to establish the lineage of Eliphaz and his descendants; finally, in Genesis 36:16, she is mentioned as an ancestor of the Edomite chiefs descended from Eliphaz. Ada is thus a genealogical link: without her, Esau's lineage and the future nation of Edom would not take the form described in the Bible.
H5711H.portee: Ada illustrates how the Bible honors mothers and women by faithfully tracing their role in the history of salvation. Although she is a Canaanite foreigner, she becomes an integral part of Esau's patriarchal genealogy, showing that God recognizes every woman as a bearer of life. Her example reminds readers that women are never mere background figures in the divine plan.

sens: Gathering of people summoned or gathered together
Group consisting of the people of Israel as a whole, or a significant part of that people
Organized Israelite community before God, particularly during religious acts
H5712.detail:
1. The word first designates a gathering of people summoned for a specific purpose. In Exodus 12:3, Moses speaks "to all the assembly of Israel" to announce the Passover: it is a call to gather for a common instruction.
2. It also refers to the people of Israel themselves, viewed as a constituted whole. In Numbers 20:1, "the whole assembly of the children of Israel" arrives at the wilderness of Zin: the word describes the entire group of people on the move.
3. Finally, it evokes the Israelite community in its religious and covenantal dimension, especially during acts of worship or judgment. In Leviticus 19:2, the Lord speaks "to all the assembly of the children of Israel" to call them to holiness: it is the people recognized as God's people, collectively responsible before Him.
H5712.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to summon" or "to gather." It describes the action of bringing people together for a common function. The same family of words expresses the idea of a fixed appointment, of an intentional assembly. It is not a chaotic crowd, but an organized group called to present themselves.
H5712.emploi: The word appears 140 times in the Old Testament, mostly in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers — the books that describe the formation and journey of the people of Israel in the wilderness. It is particularly frequent in contexts of worship (sacrifices, feasts, consecration), judgment (stoning, condemnation), and events concerning the entire people. In Numbers 16, during Korah's rebellion, the word repeatedly shows how the whole assembly is involved in the rebellion against Moses and Aaron. The assembly can sin collectively (Leviticus 4:13), receive forgiveness collectively (Numbers 15:25), or be struck by a plague (Numbers 31:16). The word always emphasizes the unity and responsibility of the group as such.
H5712.portee: This word reminds Christians that the Church itself is an "assembly" summoned by God, heir to the assembly of Israel. It shows that religious life is not individual but communal: holiness, obedience, and judgment concern the whole people. The believer cannot separate from the collective responsibility of God's people; they are part of a whole called to walk together before the Lord.

sens: What proves that something has happened or is true
Visible mark or object that attests to an agreement, a fact
Word or declaration affirming the truth of something
H5713A.detail:
1. Testimony is what serves as proof: the seven sheep that Abraham offers to Abimelech become a testimony that the well belongs to him (Genesis 21:30). It is a concrete mark that says, 'here, it happened.'
2. The word also refers to a monument or visible sign that attests to an agreement between two people. Laban and Jacob set up a heap of stones: this heap becomes a witness to their commitment not to harm one another (Genesis 31:52). The object 'speaks' in place of the men.
3. It is also the word that affirms the truth of an event. When Joshua says that the stone 'has heard' the words of God and will serve as a witness, he means that it keeps memory of the divine promise and will remind the people of their commitment (Joshua 24:27). Testimony engages the one who hears it.
H5713A.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that carries the idea of 'marking,' 'leaving a trace.' A testimony is what remains afterward, what endures and speaks. The family of this word includes the idea of repetition and permanence: the testimony is not forgotten; it continually comes back to memory.
H5713A.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, each time in a context where an object or action must 'testify' to an important fact. In all three cases, the testimony is concrete: sheep, a heap of stones, a stone. It is never just a word alone, but something visible that persists and reminds. The testimony engages future generations who will see this object.
H5713A.portee: These passages remind us that God takes our promises and commitments seriously. Visible witnesses — the things we see every day — can help us keep our vows to the Lord and to others. This invites the Christian to leave traces of faithfulness in his life: acts that testify to his love for God and his promises.

sens: Instruction or rule given by God
Divine commandment endowed with authority
Testimony of divine will
Law or ordinance to keep and observe
H5713B.detail:
1. A precept is an instruction or rule that God gives to His people. It is an authoritative word that shows what one must do. In Deuteronomy 4:45, Moses presents the precepts as part of the laws and ordinances he prescribes to the children of Israel after their exodus from Egypt.
2. The precept acts as a divine commandment that imposes itself on the one who hears it. It is not a suggestion, but an order that comes from the authority of God Himself. In Psalms 99:7, the children of Israel observed the commandments of God who spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.
3. The precept testifies to what God wants and demands, which is why it is sometimes called 'testimony' — the precept bears witness to the justice and will of God. The precepts are the deposits of divine will, what God entrusts to His people as a sacred charge.
4. The precept is a rule that must be kept, observed, known. It is not mere information, but something that engages the one who receives it. In Psalms 119:24, the psalmist says that the precepts are his delight and serve as his counselors — they guide his entire life.
H5713B.origine: The Hebrew word עֵדָה (edah) comes from a root that means 'to testify' or 'to bear witness.' The precept is therefore fundamentally a 'testimony' — that of God about what is right and good. This is why this word carries the idea that divine law does not come from arbitrary will, but testifies to the just nature of God. This same root is found in other Hebrew words related to testimony and proof.
H5713B.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Psalms and Deuteronomy. It is always in the plural and specifically refers to divine laws viewed as testimonies or commandments. The translation varies between 'precept,' 'ordinance,' 'commandment,' and 'testimony,' depending on the context and nuance to emphasize. The word is particularly frequent in Psalm 119, where it appears 21 times, expressing the psalmist's devotion to divine law: the precept is what delights him (v. 24), what he meditates on (v. 78), what he confesses and defends (v. 46, 59). The context is always one of observance, respect, and love for the divine word.
H5713B.portee: For the believer, the precept reminds us that God's commandments are not oppressive chains, but testimonies of His wisdom and justice. They are not meant to punish us, but to guide us on the right path. Meditating on the precepts, like the psalmist, is to enter into conversation with God Himself and allow His will to transform our lives.

sens: man of the time of the united monarchy
father of Achinadab, officer of Solomon
H5714G.detail: 1. Iddo is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdom of Israel was still united under Solomon. His name means 'his witness' in Hebrew. 2. He is known as the father of Achinadab, who served as an officer in Solomon's administration and was responsible for supplying the king at Mahanaim, an important city east of the Jordan (1 Kings 4:14).
H5714G.origine: The name Iddo comes from a Hebrew root meaning 'witness' or 'to attest.' It is a rather rare name in the Old Testament. This Iddo should not be confused with other characters of the same name that appear later in Israel's history, notably the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah or the seer during the time of Jeroboam.
H5714G.emploi: Iddo appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:14, in the list of the twelve officers that Solomon had established to provide for the needs of his royal household. This passage clearly situates his time in the 10th century BC, during Solomon's reign. His only known role is being the father of Achinadab, an officer of the king.

sens: Levite of the time of the divided monarchy, son of Joach
H5714H.detail: Iddo is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Gershon, the priestly branch of the tribe of Levi. He appears in the list of generations at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel and Judah. According to 1 Chronicles 6:21, he is the son of Joach and the father of Zerah, thus occupying a place in the uninterrupted chain of Levitical service at the temple.
H5714H.origine: The name Iddo means 'His Witness' in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a presence that attests or takes charge. This is the same character also called Adaiah in 1 Chronicles 6:41, showing that biblical genealogies sometimes used alternative names for the same person. Several other individuals bear this name in the Old Testament, but this one is distinguished by his place in the Levitical genealogy.
H5714H.emploi: Iddo is primarily known by his mention in 1 Chronicles 6:21, where he appears in the official genealogy of the Gershonite Levites. Although few details are given about his personal life, his inscription in this genealogical list indicates that he participated in the religious service of Israel during a pivotal period in its political history. His name also appears elsewhere in the Old Testament attached to other individuals (a father of Abinadab, a grandfather of the prophet Zechariah, a seer during the time of Jeroboam), but this entry strictly concerns the Gershonite Levite of 1 Chronicles 6:21.

sens: Prophet during the time of the divided monarchy
Author of royal records and memoirs
Figure whose testimony authenticates the accounts of the kings
H5714I.detail:
1. Iddo is a prophet who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two: the Northern Kingdom and the Southern Kingdom (Judah). The two mentions we have place him during the reigns of Rehoboam and Abijah, the first kings of Judah after the schism.
2. Iddo is known as the author or collector of royal memoirs and acts: his name appears alongside genealogical records and the official archives of the temple. In 2 Chronicles 12:15, it is said that the acts of Rehoboam are "written in the books of Shemaiah the prophet, and of Iddo the prophet."
3. Iddo's role is to document and preserve the memory of the reigns: in 2 Chronicles 13:22, the actions and words of King Abijah are reported as "written in the memoirs of the prophet Iddo." This status of prophet-scribe gives him spiritual authority over the accounts he transmits.
H5714I.origine: The name Iddo means "his witness" or "witness of God," formed from a root that evokes the idea of testimony and presence. This name is fitting for a prophet tasked with faithfully documenting the events of the reign: he is the authorized witness who records what has happened for the memory of the people.
H5714I.emploi: Iddo is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in 2 Chronicles, in chapters 12 and 13. He appears only in this brief historical window, during the early reigns of the Judah dynasty after the kingdom split. His role is exclusively that of a documentary prophet: it is through his writing that the Church of Christ knows the details of the reigns of Rehoboam and Abijah. Although he is not extensively developed in the text, his repeated and solemn mention shows that the biblical writers placed great importance on his prophetic testimony as a guarantee of the authenticity of the royal archives.
H5714I.portee: Iddo reminds us that the prophets of the Old Testament were not only preachers or miracle workers, but also guardians of memory and historical truth. His example shows that faithful testimony to the reality of events is a prophetic mission as important as proclaiming the word of God. For the believer, this invites seeing the transmission of the written Word as an act of prophetic service and trust in divine providence that preserves the memory of God's people.

sens: Grandfather of the prophet Zechariah
Man living during the time of exile and return from Babylon
H5714J.detail: Iddo is first known as the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah. Zechariah is presented as "the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo" (Zechariah 1:1), which means that Iddo was the father of Berechiah and the grandfather of Zechariah. Iddo himself is referred to as a prophet in the same verses. He appears alongside the prophet Haggai during the reconstruction of the temple after the return from Babylon, around 520 B.C. (Ezra 5:1). Iddo thus represents a line of prophetic faithfulness in the restored Jewish community: he, his son Berechiah, and his grandson Zechariah all exercised the prophetic ministry, conveying the word of the Lord to Judah and Jerusalem during this crucial period of temple reconstruction.
H5714J.origine: The Hebrew name Iddo means "his testimony" or "his witness." This meaning reflects the role of the character: Iddo is a man who testifies to the word of the Lord, first himself as a prophet, and then through his prophetic descendants.
H5714J.emploi: Iddo appears four times in Scripture, all in the books of Ezra and Zechariah, covering the beginning of the return from Babylon (around 520 B.C.). He is mentioned in Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 as a prophet prophesying to the returned Jews, alongside Haggai, to encourage them in the reconstruction of the temple. He is also named in Zechariah 1:1 and 1:7 as the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah, whose genealogy emphasizes the familial prophetic transmission. These four references highlight his key role during this period of hope and spiritual renewal after the exile.
H5714J.portee: Iddo teaches that faithfulness to God is passed down from one generation to another. As a prophet and ancestor of another major prophet, he shows how God raises up in the same family men who bear His word and serve His people. His example invites the Christian to reflect on their own spiritual heritage and their responsibility to pass on the faith to the generations that follow.

sens: Priest of the Jewish community at the return from Babylonian exile
H5714K.detail: 1. Iddo is a priest mentioned in the records of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is part of the list of priests and Levites who led the religious community after the return from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:4).
H5714K.origine: The name Iddo means "his witness" in Hebrew. It designates several characters in the Old Testament, including this priest during the time of Nehemiah who participated in the restoration of worship in Jerusalem.
H5714K.emploi: Iddo appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both passages listing the leaders of the priests during the return from exile. In Nehemiah 12:4, he is cited among the priests and Levites who came with Zerubbabel; in Nehemiah 12:16, he is mentioned again in a list of generations of priests, noting that Zechariah was his son or descendant. These lists reconstruct the line of succession of the priesthood in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.

sens: What God places before His people for them to keep and remember
The covenant and the laws that God establishes with Israel
A warning or admonition addressed by God to His people
A statute or ordinance that God imposes
The document or ark containing the divine words
H5715.detail:
1. The testimony is primarily what God "places" before His people for them to keep — it is His testimony made visible, concrete. In Exodus 40:20, it is the content of the ark: the tablets of the Law that Moses receives, material objects that embody the divine will. This ark, also called the "ark of the testimony," is the heart of the tabernacle, the place where God meets with His people (Exodus 30:36).
2. By extension, the testimony refers to the entire covenant and the laws that God has established with Israel: His commandments, His ordinances, His statutes. Psalm 78:5 states that God "established a testimony in Jacob, He set a law in Israel" — the two expressions are equivalent: the testimony is God's will for His people, codified and transmitted.
3. The testimony also carries the meaning of warning: a call to obey, to not deviate. In 2 Kings 17:15, Israel has "rejected His laws, the covenant... and the warnings He had addressed to them" — the testimony is God's message that warns, that calls to repentance.
4. It is also a statute or ordinance: a rule established by God that defines what His people must do. The ark of the tabernacle encompasses all these meanings: it contains the written testimony, it brings it to the forefront, it makes it the center of worship.
H5715.origine: The Hebrew word עֵדוּת (édut) comes from the root עוד (ud), "to bear witness" or "to repeat," which evokes the idea of reiterating, affirming what is true. A testimony is therefore what one repeats, what one asserts strongly to establish a truth. In Hebrew, the word can also mean "sign" or "proof" — what remains as a mark of truth. Here, God's testimony is His established word, which cannot be ignored, which must be repeated and taught to every generation.
H5715.emploi: The word appears 59 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the books of the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the Psalms. In the Pentateuch, it primarily designates the ark of the testimony (the chest that contains the tablets of the Law) or the tabernacle of the testimony (the sanctuary where it is placed) — this is the most concrete meaning and is most often translated as "testimony." In the Psalms, the word becomes more spiritualized: it signifies God's laws and ordinances, the precepts that must be loved and meditated upon (Psalms 119 uses this word repeatedly: "I cherish Your testimonies"). In the historical books (Kings, Chronicles), the testimony is the divine covenant that is renewed or broken, which seals the relationship between God and His king. The word slightly changes nuance depending on the context: material when it concerns the ark, legal or ethical when it concerns the laws, relational when it concerns the covenant.
H5715.portee: The testimony reminds the believer that God speaks, that He clearly establishes His will and entrusts it to His people to be kept and transmitted. It is a word that emphasizes responsibility: what God places before us is not vague or hidden, but explicit and demands to be listened to, retained, taught. For the psalmist, meditating on God's testimony becomes a joy — "Your testimonies delight me" (Psalms 119:111) — because they are the words of the One who loves us and desires our good. In Jesus Christ, this testimony becomes a living reality: He is the incarnate Word who dwells at the heart of our lives.

sens: An object or accessory that beautifies and adorns someone
A precious and ceremonial garment or attire
Harness or equipment for a horse
Physical beauty or splendor of a person
Figuratively: what is superficial or deceptive
H5716.detail: 1. An ornament is an object that one puts on oneself to appear beautiful: jewelry, accessories, clothing. In Exodus 33:4 and 33:6, the Israelites strip themselves of their ornaments as a sign of repentance and a break with the Lord: this act shows that the ornament is the external symbol of elegant adornment. 2. The adornment refers to the ensemble of coordinated ornaments, which dresses sumptuously; in Isaiah 49:18, the city of Jerusalem dresses itself with its children returned like a nuptial adornment, that is, like a complete outfit of beauty. 3. The ornaments also refer to the harness or equipment of horses: in Psalms 32:9, one "adorns" the horse with a bridle and bit, that is, one equips and controls it with accessories. 4. The ornament can evoke beauty itself, physical splendor: in Ezekiel 16:7, the young girl becomes of "perfect beauty," where the ornament refers to her natural radiance and flourishing. 5. In Jeremiah 4:30, when the city adorns itself with gold and makeup, the ornament becomes superficial and vain — it does not save the one who wears it from contempt and danger.
H5716.origine: The Hebrew word עֲדִי comes from a root that expresses the idea of embellishment and adornment. It designates everything that adorns, beautifies, equips, or adorns — whether it concerns a human being, an animal, or a city. The word appears mainly in the prophetic books, where it often contrasts between external beauty and the internal reality of sin.
H5716.emploi: The word עֲדִי appears 13 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the prophetic books (Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Isaiah) and the Psalms. In Exodus 33, removing ornaments is an act of repentance. In the Psalms, it describes the equipment of the horse or natural radiance. Among the prophets, it contrasts the brilliant appearance with inner unfaithfulness: in Ezekiel 16, Jerusalem adorns itself but forgets its God; in Jeremiah 4:30, Judah beautifies itself in vain before judgment. The ornament then becomes an indicator of spiritual superficiality.
H5716.portee: This word calls the believer to distinguish the outside from the inside. The prophets use it to show that the beauty of adornment never replaces faithfulness to God: Jerusalem may cover itself with gold, it remains abandoned if it has forsaken its God. It is a lesson in spiritual discernment: not to be seduced by appearance, either in oneself or in others.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of King Hezekiah
H5717G.detail: Adiel is a chief of the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:36. He appears in a list of Simeonite princes who lived during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. His name literally means "ornament of God," which underscores the importance of this figure in the history of Israel.
H5717G.origine: The name Adiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "adi" (ornament, adornment) and "El" (God). It expresses the idea that this person is like an adornment or ornament belonging to God, a formulation that was common for the names of leaders and nobles in Israel.
H5717G.emploi: Adiel is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:36, in a genealogical list of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of King Hezekiah. This passage enumerates the princes of Simeon and their ancestors. Adiel is listed among several other names, with no additional details about his life or actions. His unique appearance in Scripture shows the importance that the chronicler attributed to the preservation of the genealogies of the tribes of Israel.

sens: Levitical priest during the time of exile and return
Prince of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of King Hezekiah
Ancestor of the royal treasurer Azmaveth
H5717H.detail: Adiel is a proper name that designates three important figures in the history of Israel. The most well-known is the priest from the tribe of Levi mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:12, father of Maesaï; he lived during the time of the exile and the return of the people to Jerusalem. The name also appears as that of a prince of Simeon under the reign of King Hezekiah, and finally as the ancestor of Azmaveth, the officer in charge of King David's treasures. These three Adiel reflect the significance of the name in the genealogies of the chosen people.
H5717H.origine: The name Adiel means "ornament of God" or "decoration of God," composed of the Hebrew "adi" (beauty, ornament) and "el" (God). This theophoric name, which includes the divine name, expresses the idea that the bearer is a particular beauty or glory in the eyes of the Lord. It belongs to the family of Hebrew names where God is named last, like Michael or Jeremiel.
H5717H.emploi: Adiel appears in the priestly genealogies of the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Chronicles 9:12, he is identified as a Levite priest, son of Jachzéra and father of Maesaï, living at the critical time of the exile and return to Jerusalem. His inclusion in these lists shows that he was part of the recognized and established priestly families. The same name (or a variant, Azarel) appears in Nehemiah 11:13, confirming the importance of this Levitical lineage for the restored worship.
H5717H.portee: Adiel represents the continuity of priestly service through the crises of exile. His name reminds us that God continues to constitute His people as a beauty and glory among the nations, even in times of trial. The presence of Adiel in the genealogical records shows that the Lord maintains a faithful lineage for the service of the temple and communion with Him.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H5717I.detail: Adiel is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Azmaveth, who served as the treasurer of King David, responsible for overseeing all royal treasures (1 Chronicles 27:25). His name means "ornament of God" in Hebrew, but the Bible gives us no details about his personal life or specific role — we only know him through his son.
H5717I.origine: The name Adiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "adi" meaning "ornament" or "decoration," and "el" which refers to God. The name thus expresses the idea that this person is an ornament or beauty that belongs to God, a poetic way of recognizing God's glory in the one who bears this name.
H5717I.emploi: Adiel appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 27:25. He is mentioned solely as the father of Azmaveth, an important officer of King David. Azmaveth held a high position of trust: he was responsible for all the treasures of the kingdom. This unique mention suggests that Adiel came from a family of high status in the royal government, although his other activities are not recorded in the Bible.

sens: Maternal grandfather of King Josiah of Judah
Inhabitant of Botskath in the lowlands of Judah
H5718G.detail:
1. Adaja is the father of Jedidah, the mother of King Josiah of Judah (2 Kings 22:1). He is the maternal grandfather of this king who reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. This familial link connects him to the royal lineages of the kingdom of Judah during the period of the Divided Monarchy.
2. Adaja came from Botskath, a city in the lowlands (the Shephelah) of the territory of Judah. This geographical location situates his family in the agricultural and prosperous regions of southern Judah, away from the mountainous areas.
H5718G.origine: The name Adaja means in Hebrew "Jehovah has adorned" or "Jehovah has decorated" — it evokes the idea that God is clothed in beauty or majesty. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name. The name belongs to several characters in the Old Testament, including several Levites and priests, which shows its common usage in Israelite families.
H5718G.emploi: Adaja appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 22:1, where he is mentioned as the father of Jedidah and grandfather of King Josiah. It is a brief genealogical mention, identifying him through his family ties rather than by his own actions. His importance lies in his role as an ancestor of King Josiah, who will be one of the reforming kings of Judah.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H5718H.detail: Adaja is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:21. He is presented as the son of Shimei and brother of several other men (Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Beraja, and Shimrath). His name means "The Lord has adorned" or "The Lord has decorated," expressing the idea that God has beautified or glorified Himself. Although few details are given about his personal life, his genealogy situates him in the history of Israel at a time when the two kingdoms were divided. His appearance in this genealogical list of Benjamin shows that he was part of the families that continued to inhabit the northern territory of Judah after the kingdom split.
H5718H.origine: The name Adaja comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to adorn" or "to decorate," associated with the idea of beauty and glory. The composition of the name includes the divine theonym (Yah, an abbreviation of the name of God), indicating a confession of faith in the ornamental and glorious power of the Lord. It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, where the name of God is integrated into the personal name to express a relationship with the divine.
H5718H.emploi: Adaja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:21, in a genealogy of the sons of Benjamin. He is listed among the descendants of Shimei and is part of a long family list that establishes the genealogical links of the Benjaminite families. The genealogical context suggests that he was a recognized ancestor whose descendants were preserved in the records of Israel. His unique mention makes him a minor historical figure, but his presence in the chronological genealogies indicates that he had a legitimate place in the official genealogy of God's people.

sens: Priest of the tribe of Levi during the Exile and Return
H5718I.detail: Adaja is a proper name designating a Levite priest who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem. He is mentioned twice in the Bible: first in 1 Chronicles 9:12, where he is presented as the son of Jerocham, and a second time in Nehemiah 11:12, where an Adaja son of Jerocham also appears. These two mentions make him an important figure of the clergy during the reconstruction of the temple after the exile to Babylon.
H5718I.origine: The name Adaja means "Jehovah has adorned" or "Jehovah has decorated": it expresses the idea that God has adorned or beautified Himself, a poetic formula to say that God has manifested or taken care. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name (Yah, a short form of the name God), which was common among Levitical families in the Old Testament.
H5718I.emploi: Adaja appears twice in the biblical texts: in 1 Chronicles 9:12 and in Nehemiah 11:12. Both passages list the priests and Levites who returned from the Exile to Babylon to ensure the worship of the restored temple. In these genealogical lists, Adaja is presented as a respectable member of the priestly lineage, son of Jerocham. His appearance in these two contexts emphasizes the importance of genealogical continuity and the religious role of Levitical families after the return from exile.

sens: A man of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Father of Maaséja, one of the captains who supported the priest Jehoiada
H5718J.detail:
1. Adaja is a figure mentioned in the history of the kingdom of Judah, at a time when the kingdom was divided between Judah and Israel. His name appears in the context of significant events involving leaders and priests.
2. He is known as the father of Maaséja, who was one of the military captains involved in a crucial alliance with the priest Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 23:1). These officers played a decisive role in the religious and political events of Judah during that time.
H5718J.origine: The name Adaja means "The Lord has adorned" or "The Lord has beautified," composed of the divine name (Yah) and a verb evoking embellishment or adornment. It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, confessing the action or excellence of God. Several individuals bore this name in the history of Israel, which was common for meaningful names.
H5718J.emploi: Adaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 23:1, as the father of Maaséja. This Maaséja was among the captains who, under the leadership of the priest Jehoiada, plotted a decisive alliance to restore legitimate order in Judah. His appearance in this context shows that Adaja had descendants involved in the major affairs of the temple and the Judean government.

sens: A man of the descendants of Bani who married a foreign woman during the time of Ezra
H5718K.detail: 1. Adaja is a man mentioned at the return from Exile, among the descendants of Bani (an important family of Judah) who had married foreign women. This practice was forbidden by the Law, and Ezra ordered them to separate from their non-Israelite wives to preserve the purity of the people returned to the promised land (Ezra 10:29).
H5718K.origine: The name Adaja comes from Hebrew and means "The Lord has adorned" or "Jehovah has adorned Himself." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God (Yah or Jehovah) as a constitutive element, which was common among the Hebrews. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel, but this one is distinguished by its historical context and genealogy.
H5718K.emploi: Adaja appears only once in the biblical text of the Segond, in Ezra 10:29. He is mentioned in the list of men who, after the return from the Babylonian Exile, had to send away their foreign wives, in accordance with the religious reform led by Ezra. This list is a historical testimony of a major crisis in the restoration of Israel: the issue of mixed marriages and the religious identity of the people returned from captivity.

sens: A man who lived during the time of the Exile and the return
A descendant of Bani who married a foreign woman
H5718L.detail:
1. Adaja is a proper name designating a man living during the time of the Exile and the return from exile to Judea. He appears in the list of men who, under the leadership of Ezra, acknowledged having sinned by marrying foreign women and promised to repudiate them. He is one of the many names in this list from Ezra 10, where the people returned from captivity seek to purify themselves by conforming to the Law.
2. More specifically, Adaja was a descendant of the family of Bani and was among those who had contracted mixed marriages during the exile or upon return. His inclusion in this list shows that he recognized this transgression and committed to correcting his situation.
H5718L.origine: The Hebrew name Adaja (עֲדָיָהוּ) literally means "Yhwh (God) has adorned" or "God has beautified." It is composed of roots that evoke ornament and adornment. This name, borne by several characters in the history of Israel, expressed a confession of faith: the one who bore it recognized that God alone is clothed in glory and majesty.
H5718L.emploi: Adaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:39, in the list of those who renounced their mixed marriages after the return from exile. This occurrence corresponds to the context of national and religious restoration under the leadership of Ezra, when the Jewish people, freshly returned from Babylon, undertook to conform to the Law of Moses. Although this is a unique mention in the preserved biblical text, the name Adaja likely also designates other characters referenced in the genealogy of Israel, including a grandfather of King Josiah and a Levite from the family of Gershon.

sens: A character of Israel during the return from exile
H5718M.detail: Adaja is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:5. He is the father of Hazaja and the son of Jojarib. This man belongs to the lineage of the inhabitants of Jerusalem who resettled after the exile to Babylon, at the time of the restoration of the people of Israel.
H5718M.origine: The name Adaja means "The Lord has adorned" or "The Lord has beautified," composed of Hebrew terms expressing the idea that God Himself has beautified or glorified. This name expresses praise to God and reflects the faith of the parents who gave this name to their child.
H5718M.emploi: Adaja is mentioned only in Nehemiah 11:5, in the context of the census of families who resettled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He appears as an ancestor of Maaséja, one of the inhabitants of the holy city at the time of Nehemiah. His name appears in a genealogy establishing the continuity of the people of Israel despite the exile and dispersion.

sens: A Levite character of the Old Testament
H5718N.detail: Adaja is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in the genealogical line of the temple musicians: son of Ethni and father of Zerah, he is part of the succession of the ancestors of Asaph, the famous choir leader of the temple in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 6:41). His name literally means "The Lord has adorned" or "The Lord has beautified," expressing the idea that God has magnified or glorified Himself. This Levite is part of those temple genealogies that the book of Chronicles enumerates to establish the legitimacy of religious functions during the reigns of the kings of Judah.
H5718N.origine: The name Adaja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "adi" (ornament, adornment) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name the Lord). It belongs to the family of theophoric names, that is, names incorporating the name of God, which were very common in Israel. These names generally expressed trust or a prayer to the Lord.
H5718N.emploi: Adaja is a character from the Levitical genealogies, mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a member of the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy. He is listed in the direct line of those who served in the temple, particularly in the musical class. The text of 1 Chronicles 6:41 situates him precisely in the genealogical succession: he is the son of Ethni and the father of Zerah, which would make him a distant ancestor of the temple musicians.

sens: One who delights in sensual and carnal pleasures
One who lives in luxury and carefreeness
One who displays a proud confidence in their wealth
H5719.detail:
1. The word describes a person who indulges in sensual and carnal pleasures, without restraint or moderation. In Isaiah 47:8, it applies to personified Babylon, which gives itself over to the satisfaction of its desires.

2. It also evokes a life of luxury and carefreeness, far from worries and fears. Babylon sits "with assurance," forgetting the threats that will come upon her.

3. The word can finally express a carnal, proud confidence that rests on power and wealth rather than on God. Babylon says, "Me, and nothing but me!", certain of its invulnerability.
H5719.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of sweetness and softness. It belongs to the family of terms that describe carnal well-being and a lack of vigilance. Its biblical use connects it to a dangerous spiritual attitude: that of a heart that falls asleep in material abundance and forgets God.
H5719.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 47:8, where the prophet rebukes Babylon for its pride and luxury. He addresses the great earthly power that reigns without apparent rival and believes it can escape God's judgment. Through this unique qualifier, the prophet exposes the heart of Babylon: a voluptuous confidence in itself, completely cut off from the reality of the judgment that awaits it.
H5719.portee: This word invites Christians to guard against carnal security, the comfort that dulls spiritual vigilance. Babylon represents every human system that rises against God and believes in its own permanence. The warning still resonates: voluptuousness and pride are the precursors to a fall. Trusting in God rather than in one's own strength is the path to wisdom.

sens: Man from the period of Exile and Return
Head of a family of exiles who returned with Zerubbabel
Signatory of the covenant with Nehemiah
H5720G.detail: Adin is a character from the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem, after the Babylonian captivity. His name literally means "delicate" or "refined". He is first mentioned as the ancestor of a large family of exiles: upon their return with Zerubbabel, the descendants of Adin formed a group of four hundred fifty-four people (Ezra 2:15). Later, during the return of a second wave with Ezra, one of Adin's sons, the chief Ebed, son of Jonathan, leads fifty men from his family (Ezra 8:6). The name also appears in Nehemiah's list, where the sons of Adin number six hundred fifty-five, and where Adin is among the leaders who sign the solemn covenant with God (Nehemiah 7:20). These lists show that Adin was an important man, founder of an influential family line among the returned exiles.
H5720G.origine: The Hebrew name עָדִין (Adin) derives from a root evoking what is delicate, refined, or tender. It is a characteristic name from the Second Temple period, borne by a prominent family at the return from exile.
H5720G.emploi: Adin appears three times in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, both dedicated to the return of the exiles and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The first mention designates him as the ancestor of an important family of exiles (Ezra 2:15). He is then cited during the return with Ezra, where one of his descendants leads a family group (Ezra 8:6). Finally, he appears in the parallel list of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:20), before being counted among the signatories of the covenant. These three occurrences paint the portrait of a significant man in the return community, whose family played a leadership role.

sens: Leader of the exiles returned from Babylon
Ancestor of a family of exiles
H5720H.detail: Adin is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile. He is a leader among the exiles who left Babylon to return to Jerusalem under the leadership of Zerubbabel. His name means "delicate" or "refined" in Hebrew. In Nehemiah 10:16, he is among the leaders who signed the solemn covenant with Nehemiah, committing to observe the law of Moses and to maintain the restored community in obedience to God. This act of signing the covenant shows the importance of his role in the religious and civil reorganization of Judah after the exile.
H5720H.origine: The name Adin comes from Hebrew and literally means "delicate" or "dainty", evoking someone refined or tender. This root suggests a certain finesse or delicacy. In the Old Testament, names often carry a meaning that reflects qualities or circumstances of birth; here, the name might have designated a person of noble condition or distinguished character.
H5720H.emploi: Adin is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 10:16. He appears in the list of the people's leaders who affixed their seal to the covenant document made under Nehemiah, after the return from the Babylonian exile. His presence in this official list indicates that he was a recognized authority figure among the returned exiles. He embodies one of the families that survived the exile and played a role in the restoration of the Jewish community in Jerusalem.
H5720H.portee: Adin represents the faithful leaders who, upon returning from exile, took the solemn commitment to live according to God's Law. His example reminds us that the spiritual restoration of a community relies on the personal commitment of those who lead it. The signing of the covenant shows how leaders must walk before the people in obedience to God.

sens: Chief of the Reubenites under King David
H5721.detail: Adina is a Reubenite military chief who served King David. He is mentioned as the son of Shiza and commanded thirty men under David's orders (1 Chronicles 11:42). His name appears among the mighty warriors and leaders of David, indicating his high rank in the royal army of that time.
H5721.origine: The name "Adina" means "slender" or "graceful" in Hebrew. Although the exact etymology is debated, it evokes the idea of a delicate or fine person. It is a typical Hebrew name from the Second Temple period and biblical times, borne by characters of high social rank.
H5721.emploi: Adina appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:42, where he is presented as one of David's military leaders during the divided monarchy period. He is listed among the mighty men of David who supported and followed him. His role was to command the Reubenites, the tribe from which he originated, within the royal army. This unique mention firmly situates him in the context of the warriors and military administrators of King David.

sens: One of the mighty warriors of King David
H5722.detail: Adino is a warrior from the time of King David, mentioned only once in the Bible. His name means "his ornament" in Hebrew, suggesting that he was a remarkable man worthy of distinction. He appears in the list of David's "mighty men" or "valiant warriors" (2 Samuel 23:8), an elite group that served directly under the king and distinguished themselves by their bravery and strength in battle.
H5722.origine: The name Adino comes from Hebrew and literally means "his ornament". It is formed from a root that evokes beauty, brilliance, and dignity — the idea of something or someone that adorns. For David, such a warrior represented indeed an ornament, a glory for his army and for his reign.
H5722.emploi: Adino appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:8, within the catalog of David's renowned warriors. He is ranked among the king's most valiant fighters, those who participated in his victories and formed the core of his army. This unique mention suggests that he was a well-known figure during King David's time, but whose specific exploits have not been recorded in the preserved biblical texts.
H5722.portee: This name reminds us that service to God and the king can be accomplished in relative anonymity. Adino was a courageous warrior, worthy of being part of the military elite, but biblical history has preserved only his name. This invites the reader to understand that faithfulness and courage in the background, without particular glory, also hold value in God's eyes.

sens: City in the lowland of Judah
H5723.detail: Adithaïm is a small town located in the low and fertile region of Judah, at the foot of the hills bordering the Mediterranean coast. It appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:36).
H5723.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "double ornament" or "my double adornment": it is composed of two elements that evoke something embellished or adorned. This name was held by a modest locality in the coastal region of Judah, probably a fortified site or a prosperous agricultural establishment.
H5723.emploi: Adithaïm is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 15, where the complete list of cities of the tribe of Judah is enumerated after the conquest of the land. It is among the villages of the Shephelah, this intermediate area between the Judean mountains and the coastal plain. Its unique mention shows that it was a second-tier city in the territorial judgment of Judah.

sens: man from the time of the divided monarchy, father of Shaphat
H5724.detail: Adlaï is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Shaphat, who served King David as the overseer of the herds of cattle in the valleys (1 Chronicles 27:29). His name appears in the list of officials responsible for the administration of royal property under David.
