H5724.origine: The name Adlaï literally means "justice of Jehovah": it is composed of two Hebrew elements expressing the idea of justice and invoking the divine name. It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes the name of God, like many ancient Hebrew names.
H5724.emploi: Adlaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:29. He is simply cited as the father of Shaphat, one of the twelve officials that David had appointed to manage his property and herds. This passage is part of an administrative enumeration; Adlaï himself is not an active character in the narrative, but merely a genealogical link.

sens: City of the lowlands of Judah, formerly Canaanite
Place where David hid while fleeing Saul
Natural cave serving as a refuge
H5725.detail:
1. Adullam was a fortified city located in the low hills of Judah, west of Jerusalem. It had originally belonged to the Canaanites before being conquered and assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:35 mentions it among the cities of Judah; 2 Chronicles 11:7 shows that it was fortified later).
2. The city is especially famous as a place of refuge: David, fleeing the jealousy of King Saul, escaped to the cave of Adullam, and his brothers and family came to join him there (1 Samuel 22:1). It was a safe and secluded place where he could escape his pursuers.
3. This cave became a rallying point for David's loyal warriors: three of his thirty chiefs came down to see him in this cave when the Philistines camped nearby (2 Samuel 23:13 and 1 Chronicles 11:15). It thus embodies the refuge of the innocent persecuted, protected by the hand of God.
H5725.origine: The name means "justice of the people" in Hebrew. Adullam was an ancient Canaanite settlement whose strategic importance lay in its position in the hills and especially in its natural cave, which offered a natural refuge. The derivative "Adullamite" (Joshua 12:15) designates an inhabitant or native of this city.
H5725.emploi: Adullam appears 8 times in the Bible. It is first a Canaanite city conquered and integrated into the territory of Judah during the division of the land (Joshua 12:15 and 15:35). It becomes historically famous during David's flight: it is there that he took refuge and where his family found him (1 Samuel 22:1). After his ascension as king, David returned there with his elite warriors (2 Samuel 23:13 and 1 Chronicles 11:15), showing its continued importance. It is also listed among the fortified cities of the kingdom of Judah (2 Chronicles 11:7) and the locations reoccupied after the exile (Nehemiah 11:30).
H5725.portee: Adullam symbolizes the refuge of one who suffers unjustly. The cave where David found protection becomes the biblical image of the place where God hides the persecuted. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that in times of distress and isolation, even in the darkness of a cave, God does not abandon them and provides a safe refuge. It is an encouragement for those facing opposition or injustice.

sens: inhabitant of the city of Adullam
friend or companion of a person from this place
H5726.detail:
1. An Adullamite is someone who comes from or lives in the city of Adullam, in Judah. It is a place name used to identify a person by their geographical origin, much like saying "a Parisian" or "a Marseillais". In Genesis 38:1, Judah withdraws to "a man of Adullam", indicating that the city exists and its inhabitants are known.
2. By extension, the word can refer to a companion or friend associated with someone from the place. Hira, Judah's friend, is called "the Adullamite" (Genesis 38:12 and 38:20): the term identifies his origin and thus connects him to Judah in a relationship of friendship and business.
H5726.origine: The word comes from the name of the city of Adullam (in Hebrew Adoullam), whose traditional meaning is "justice of the people". This city was a fortress in southern Judah, known during the patriarchal era. The Adullamite is simply "one from Adullam", formed by adding the gentilic suffix that designates the inhabitant of a place.
H5726.emploi: The term appears only three times in the Bible, all in Genesis 38, in the story of Judah and Tamar. It exclusively refers to Hira, Judah's friend and companion. This man acts as an intermediary: he accompanies Judah to Timnah for the sheep shearing (Genesis 38:12), and he is sent by Judah to retrieve a pledge (Genesis 38:20). His title "the Adullamite" emphasizes that he is an established resident of the region, perhaps a business partner or a trusted guide for Judah, who is himself a stranger in the land at that time.

sens: To indulge in pleasure and physical satisfaction
To enjoy abundantly goods and food
To live in comfort and material satisfaction
H5727.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of indulgently surrendering to pleasure: it is to take delight in something, to enjoy it fully and without restraint. In Nehemiah 9:25, the people of Israel, after conquering the promised land, "delighted in abundance" — they reveled in the riches, abundant harvests, and comfortable homes that God gave them.
2. Concretely, the word designates the action of enjoying material goods: possessing vineyards, olive trees, full houses, eating to satisfaction. It is the image of a life of comfort and abundance where all needs are met and exceeded.
3. In a broader figurative sense, it is to live in complete satisfaction, in well-being without worry — a form of enjoyment that can include gratitude towards God or, conversely, forgetting Him if prosperity diverts the heart from dependence on the One who is its source.
H5727.origine: The Hebrew verb עָדַן comes from a root expressing sweetness, pleasure, and delight. It is related to Eden (עֵדֶן / Eden), the garden of delights that God created at the beginning — a word that carries the idea of a place of luxury, comfort, and perfect satisfaction. The form used here (Hithpael) adds to the root the idea of indulgently surrendering to it, of taking pleasure in it.
H5727.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 9:25. It is found in the confession prayer of the people: after enumerating all of God's blessings — fertile lands, cities, harvests, fresh water — Israel acknowledges that it has delighted in these gifts. This context reveals the important nuance of the word: it is not inherently negative, but it carries a tension. The people enjoyed the divine blessings and forgot them; they indulged in well-being without remembering the God who had given them. It is a verb of contrast: the Israelites ate, were satisfied, grew fat, and delighted "by your great goodness" — but this enumeration leads to the recognition that they subsequently disobeyed (verse 26 and following).
H5727.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on their relationship to goods and material comfort. To delight in divine gifts is not wrong in itself — God gives abundance for us to enjoy — but the danger is forgetting the Giver. Nehemiah's prayer warns us: prosperity can draw us away from God if we do not maintain a grateful and obedient heart. It is a lesson for us: how do we receive the blessings that God grants us? With gratitude and faithfulness, or in forgetfulness of His goodness?

sens: Up to now, up to this moment
Always, continuously
Not yet, not... yet
H5728.detail:
1. The word marks a point in time: an action or state that has lasted from before until now, without ceasing. In Ecclesiastes 4:2, "the living who are still alive" refers to those who continue to live, who have not ceased to live.
2. It also expresses continuity or permanence — something that persists, that remains true. It is the idea that the described state has not changed up to now.
3. With a negation ("has not yet existed"), it expresses absence up to now, the idea that something has not occurred and has not taken place (Ecclesiastes 4:3).
H5728.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "continuing" or "persisting." It is a temporal adverb that anchors an action or state in duration up to the present moment. The family of words around this root often evokes the idea of what remains or subsists.
H5728.emploi: This word appears twice in Ecclesiastes, in the passage where the wise man reflects on happiness and misfortune. It is used to emphasize continuity: "still alive" (4:2) refers to those who are still living, and "has not yet existed" (4:3) means has never existed up to this day. In this context of wisdom and meditation on the human condition, the adverb creates a tension between life that continues and the desire to have or not have lived. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, limited to this passage.
H5728.portee: For the reader, this word highlights the reality of the present moment and the importance of "up to now." In the melancholic reflection of Ecclesiastes, it helps to focus attention on the continuity of suffering or life, inviting consideration of how the persistent present shapes our judgment on existence.

sens: Region of northwestern Mesopotamia conquered by Assyria
Commercial and prosperous territory around the Assyrian kingdom
H5729.detail: 1. Eden is a historical region in northwestern Mesopotamia that the Assyrians conquered and incorporated into their empire. When the king of Assyria lists his victories in 2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12, he mentions "the sons of Eden" among the territories and peoples he has subdued, alongside Gozan, Haran, and Retseph: it is an act of military and political conquest. 2. Ezekiel 27:23 presents it as a prosperous trading center that traded with Tyre, alongside Haran, Canneh, Sheba, and Assyria: Eden appears here not as a defeated adversary, but as an important economic partner, a place of trade and merchant exchanges.
H5729.origine: The name "Eden" means "pleasure" in Hebrew. This region bears this evocative name, probably because it was fertile and prosperous, or because the ancients viewed it as a land of abundance. It should not be confused with the historical region of the garden of Eden in the book of Genesis, although both share the same Hebrew name: the garden of Eden is the divine creation at the beginning of the world, while Eden here is a political and commercial territory of the first millennium BCE.
H5729.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, only in texts related to Assyrian power. Twice (2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12), the king of Assyria boasts of having defeated the deities and nations, including the "sons of Eden" — an ancient way of referring to a region as a political entity with its inhabitants. A third time (Ezekiel 27:23), the prophet lists the trading partners of Tyre, and Eden appears as an active trading center. The political and commercial significance of this region is clearly evident from these three uses.
H5729.portee: Eden reminds us that God knows and governs all the kingdoms of the earth, even the most powerful. When the prophet Isaiah reports the boasts of the king of Assyria (Isaiah 37:12), he prepares the reader to discover how only God can deliver His people from this threat. The fall of this renowned empire shows that no human power, however great, can stand against the Lord.

sens: What pleases the senses, what is pleasant and sought after
The precious goods, the treasures of a person or a country
What brings joy, satisfaction, abundance
H5730A.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes what pleases the senses: magnificent clothing, jewelry, fine fabrics — what one seeks for elegance and beauty. In 2 Samuel 1:24, the daughters of Israel wear crimson garments adorned with gold: these are the delights of royal adornment.
2. By extension, it also refers to what is precious and of great value: the treasures and goods of a nation. Jeremiah 51:34 speaks of the precious riches of Jerusalem that the king of Babylon has devoured, as if a dragon were swallowing the best of its prey.
3. In a figurative and broader sense, it is the very abundance that brings joy and satisfaction: the water that refreshes, the house full of goods (Psalms 36:9). The word then expresses the blessing and prosperity that fill with joy.
H5730A.origine: This Hebrew word originally designates what pleases, what is sweet to the touch or sight. It is related to the idea of delight and refinement. The word appears infrequently in biblical Hebrew, but its usage shows the importance given to what is beautiful, precious, and a source of satisfaction — not out of superficiality, but because the beauty and order of creation reflect the goodness of God.
H5730A.emploi: The word appears only three times in classical biblical Hebrew. It first describes the luxuries of royalty: sumptuous clothing (2 Samuel 1:24). It then denotes the material wealth of a nation: the treasures that Babylon plunders (Jeremiah 51:34). Finally, it expresses the satisfaction and joy that come from divine abundance (Psalms 36:9), where the believer is satisfied with the house of the Lord. In each case, it is what is beautiful, precious, and a source of joy.
H5730A.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the beauty of creation and the generosity of God who provides for our needs. But it also poses a question: where do we seek our delights? In fleeting ornaments and riches that can be lost, or in the abundance and presence of God that fills the soul? True delights are not vain luxury, but the experience of divine grace.

sens: Physical or sensual pleasure, longing to enjoy
Wish, expectation of satisfaction
H5730B.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes physical pleasure or carnal enjoyment: it is the desire to taste sensual pleasures. In Genesis 18:12, when Sarah laughs to herself saying, "Am I still to have this pleasure?", she is thinking of marital pleasure — which is only possible if she is young and able to conceive.
2. More broadly, it encompasses any wish, any longing to satisfy an aspiration, a need, or a project. In the same verse, Sarah doubts not only her ability to experience physical desire but also her hope of ever bearing children, which reflects a deep expectation — a desire in the broadest sense of the term.
H5730B.origine: The Hebrew word עֶדְנָה (édnah) belongs to the family of the root עדן which evokes sweetness, pleasure, and abundance. It is found in "Eden" (Genesis 2:8), the garden of pleasure and delight, where Adam and Eve enjoyed all that God had created. It is a word that carries the image of what is pleasant, sweet to the taste, or enjoyable to experience.
H5730B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 18:12. Sarah, who is ninety years old and whose body is worn out by age, laughs inwardly upon learning that she will bear a child. She wonders if she can still have desire — particularly marital desire, which is a condition for the relationship that could make her pregnant. It is a moment filled with sad irony: Sarah doubts that her desire can still awaken and that her body can respond to this call.
H5730B.portee: This word reminds us that our desires — whether physical, relational, or spiritual — tell us something profound about what we expect and what we truly wish for. Sarah doubts that her old age can still know desire, that is, still hope and life. Yet, God promises the impossible: He revives desire, He restores what age seemed to have killed. It is a lesson on the power of God in the face of our limitations.

sens: Levite man, father or ancestor in the Gershonite tribe
H5731A.detail: 1. Eden is a Levite who appears during the religious reforms of King Hezekiah, around the 8th century BCE. He is mentioned as the son of Joach and belongs to the family of the Gershonites, one of the three main branches of the tribe of Levi responsible for temple service (2 Chronicles 29:12).
H5731A.origine: The Hebrew name Eden literally means "pleasure" or "delight" — it is also the name of the wonderful garden where God placed Adam and Eve at the beginning of Creation. The same root word evokes the idea of sweetness and abundance. Although the biblical text tells us nothing more about him, this character bears a name loaded with this positive meaning.
H5731A.emploi: Eden is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12, at the time when King Hezekiah mobilizes the Levites to clean and restore the temple that previous kings had allowed to fall into ruin. He appears in a list of officiating Levites, alongside other faithful servants of the Lord during a great religious reform. He is an example of those temple servants whose memory the Bible simply preserves in its genealogical lists.

sens: Paradisiacal garden where God placed man at creation
Place of delights and abundance
Biblical image of lost perfection to be restored
H5731B.detail:
1. Eden is the garden that God planted "in the east" after creating man (Genesis 2:8). It is the first home of humanity, where Adam was given the mission to cultivate and keep this place of life (Genesis 2:15). After sin, man was expelled from it, and armed cherubim guard the access (Genesis 3:24).
2. The name literally means "pleasure" or "delight": it is a garden of abundance, where all the "trees of Eden" evoke envy in the observer due to their remarkable beauty and fertility (Ezekiel 31:9). It is the biblical model of the lost paradise.
3. The prophets of God's people invoke it as an image of hope: God promises to transform the desert of Zion into a garden like Eden, restoring joy and gladness (Isaiah 51:3). The return of the exiled people is described as a return to Eden (Ezekiel 36:35).
H5731B.origine: The Hebrew word עֵדֶן literally means "pleasure" or "delight". It designates the primordial garden where God wanted man to live in communion with Him, free, nourished, and at peace. The name is specific to the biblical world: it embodies the original human happiness as imagined by the faith of Israel.
H5731B.emploi: Eden appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in two main passages. First in the account of Genesis 2-4, where it is the garden of creation and the site of Adam's first sin. Then, in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Joel), where Eden becomes an image of restoration: Eden represents the state of perfection that God wants to restore for His people. In Ezekiel, the King of Tyre is compared to the trees of Eden in their glory before being destroyed (Ezekiel 31:18), which shows that Eden also symbolizes past splendor and defeated pride.
H5731B.portee: Eden speaks to the Christian of the beauty of God's original design for humanity: to live in peace, abundance, and communion with God, without fear and without guilt. The lost paradise reminds every reader that there is a rupture between what God wanted for us and what we have realized through sin. But the promise of restoration — a return to beauty, joy, and divine order — runs throughout the Bible and culminates in the vision of the new Heaven where God will dwell with men. Eden is therefore not simply a regretted past, but the announcement of a redeemed future.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi living during the time of the Divided Kingdom
H5731G.detail: 1. Eden is a Levitical priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of the Divided Kingdom (around the 8th century BC). He was responsible, along with others, for faithfully distributing the offerings and tithes to the priests and Levites of his people, according to their respective divisions (2 Chronicles 31:15).
H5731G.origine: The name Eden literally means "pleasure" or "delight" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of well-being and satisfaction. This same name refers to the Garden of Eden, the first dwelling place that God gave to man after creation. Thus, the priest bore a name rich with this biblical resonance of rest and divine blessing.
H5731G.emploi: Eden appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 31:15, as one of the administrators of the distributions of tithes and offerings at the temple during the religious reforms of the Kingdom of Judah. The Bible provides no further details about his life or ministry.

sens: Duration, lapse of time that passes
Specific moment, particular instant when something happens
Period, era characterized by certain events
Circumstances, historical or political situation
H5732.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a duration that passes, a sequence of moments that go by. In Daniel 4:16, "seven times shall pass over him" refers to the years that accumulate and gradually pass over the head of the king.
2. It can also mark a particular instant, a precise point in the unfolding of events — the moment when something is to occur. In Daniel 3:5, "at the moment you hear the sound of the trumpet" sets the exact signal at which the people must bow down.
3. The word can encompass an entire period marked by changes or common characteristics. In Daniel 2:21, "the times are changed" speaks of those periods that succeed one another in history.
4. Finally, "time" can refer to the circumstances and events that mark an era, the political or historical situation that prevails. This meaning is understood when the king tells the wise men that they want to "buy time" in Daniel 2:8 — they seek to postpone the moment of judgment.
H5732.origine: The Hebrew word עִדָּן (iddan) is of Aramaic origin, a language spoken in Babylon. It expresses the idea of time passing, of the succession of moments. The word belongs to the vocabulary of the Book of Daniel, largely composed in Aramaic, and appears exclusively in this book of the Bible. It is close to Semitic roots that evoke the regular return of seasons and cycles.
H5732.emploi: The word iddan appears 11 times, all in the Book of Daniel (chapters 2, 3, 4, and 7). It is used in the accounts of Nebuchadnezzar's reign and in Daniel's visions. In Daniel 2:8-9, it speaks of the delay that the wise men want to gain and the future changes of times. In Daniel 3:5 and 3:15, it designates the precise moment when the music is to sound. In Daniel 4:16, 4:23, 4:25, and 4:32, it refers to the "seven times" — a period of punishment for the king. In Daniel 7:12 and 7:25, it applies to the periods of kingdoms in the apocalyptic visions. The meaning of the word remains consistent: it always refers to a duration or a moment, but the context colors its use — sometimes a larger scale (the years of punishment), sometimes a smaller scale (the instant when the trumpet sounds).
H5732.portee: This word reminds us that time is under God's control: in Daniel 2:21, it is He who "changes times and seasons." For the believer, this means that the periods of history, even chaotic or threatening, are not left to chance. The "seven times" of Nebuchadnezzar's punishment also show that God measures the time of His judgments precisely. Finally, the frequent use of the word in apocalyptic visions invites us to recognize that the future belongs solely to God.

sens: Man from the family of Pachath-Moab who returned with Ezra
One who had married a foreign woman and had to repudiate her
H5733G.detail:
1. Adna is a man belonging to the family of Pachath-Moab, one of the great families of Israel. He is among those who returned from Babylonian exile with the scribe Ezra, probably in the 5th century BC (Ezra 10:30).
2. Adna had committed the same sin as many of his compatriots who returned: he had married a foreign woman, that is, a woman who did not follow the faith of Israel. Ezra, horrified by this transgression of the Law, compelled all men in this situation to repudiate their foreign wives and send away their children: Adna had to obey this strict order.
H5733G.origine: The name Adna means "rest" or "pleasure" in Hebrew. It is formed from a root that expresses rest, relaxation, well-being — an image of peace and contentment. This name was borne by at least two characters in Israel's history, but only this one is mentioned in detail by the Bible.
H5733G.emploi: Adna appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:30. The context is that of the return from exile: Ezra discovers that many men, including among the leaders and priests, have married foreign women in violation of the Law (Exodus 34:16, Deuteronomy 7:3). Ezra organizes a solemn assembly and forces all these men to repudiate their foreign wives. Adna is listed among the sons of Pachath-Moab who comply with this drastic edict. His name appears in a simple list, with no further details about his life or personal reaction.
H5733G.portee: The story of Adna illustrates the tension between human love and obedience to divine Law. It also shows the terrible price of sin and unfaithfulness: families torn apart to restore the purity of the people. For the Christian reader, this account invites reflection on the seriousness of marriage according to God (2 Corinthians 6:14) and on the real cost of separation from sin.

sens: Man from the period of exile and the return to Jerusalem
H5733H.detail: Adna is a priest from the family of Harim, living during the time of the return from exile under Nehemiah. The context of Nehemiah 12:15 mentions him among the leaders of the priestly families at the time of Joiakim, son of Jeshua, responsible for leading the religious life of the rebuilt community.
H5733H.origine: The name Adna means "rest" or "delight" in Hebrew, evoking calmness and satisfaction. It belongs to the post-exilic period when the Israelites return from Babylonian captivity and restore worship in Jerusalem.
H5733H.emploi: Adna appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:15. He is mentioned as one of the leaders of the priestly family of Harim during the time of Joiakim. This context places him in the generations that followed the return of the people of Judah after the Babylonian exile, a crucial moment of reorganization of worship and Jewish communal life.

sens: military leader during the time of the divided monarchy
H5734G.detail: Adnah is a man from the clan of Manasseh (one of the twelve tribes of Israel) who, during the reign of Saul over Israel, deserts the royal army to join David at Ziklag, a city in the south. He becomes one of David's loyal warriors during his flight and rise to power.
H5734G.origine: The name Adnah literally means "pleasure" or "delight" in Hebrew. It derives from the root עדן (eden), which evokes sweetness and pleasantness, and which also appears in the word "Eden," the garden of God.
H5734G.emploi: Adnah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:20. The text mentions him among the leaders of Manasseh who join David at Ziklag, at the time when he is fleeing from King Saul. His presence in the list of David's warriors shows his importance as a military officer during the transition between Saul's reign and David's.

sens: military officer of the kingdom of Judah
commander of a large army
H5734H.detail:
1. Adna is a military leader of Judah who appears only once in the Bible, during the counting of the troops under King Jehoshaphat. He is listed as the head of the chiefs of thousands of Judah, indicating that he held a high rank in the military hierarchy (2 Chronicles 17:14).
2. He commanded three hundred thousand valiant men, making him one of the most powerful generals in the kingdom at that time. This number demonstrates the importance of his position and the trust that the king placed in him to defend the kingdom of Judah.
H5734H.origine: The name Adna means "pleasure" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes satisfaction and joy. It is a rare name in the Old Testament, borne by this one officer mentioned in Chronicles.
H5734H.emploi: Adna is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:14. He appears in the context of King Jehoshaphat's reign, who had strengthened the army of Judah and reorganized its military forces. The text presents him as the first of the chiefs of thousands, suggesting that he was the highest-ranking among the commanders listed at that time.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H5735.detail: Adada is a city located in the far south of the territory of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the conquest. It appears between Kina and Dimona, both located in the Negev, the desert region of the south.
H5735.origine: The Hebrew name עֲדְעָדָה (Adada) could mean "festival" or "boundary place" according to some interpretations, although the exact etymology remains uncertain. This type of geographical name was common in ancient Israel to designate localities of little importance, especially in peripheral regions like the Negev.
H5735.emploi: Adada is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua in chapter 15, in the detailed list of cities and towns that belonged to the tribe of Judah. This list, given after the conquest of Canaan, systematically enumerates the localities of the Judean territory from north to south. Adada, located in the far south, testifies to the extent of the territory conquered by Judah, up to the borders of the Negev desert.

H5736.fr: to exceed or remain in surplus
sens: What exceeds a fixed quantity, what surpasses
What remains after a distribution or use
The excess of a measure or account
To have more than necessary, to be in excess
H5736.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what exceeds a limit: in Numbers 3:46, when counting the firstborn of Israel, some numbers "exceed" that of the Levites, meaning there are more than necessary for the exchange.
2. It also signifies what remains after an operation: in Exodus 16:23, the manna that "remains" until morning must be set aside; in Leviticus 25:27, the buyer receives the "surplus" he must pay, which is the money that exceeds the base price.
3. In measures and dimensions, it is the portion of fabric that "remains" beyond what is necessary: in Exodus 26:12-13, the tent's curtains have a "surplus" and a "remainder" that hang over the sides of the tabernacle to cover it completely.
4. The word also expresses the idea of being in excess: in Exodus 16:18, he who gathered more manna "had nothing left over," in other words, he had no surplus.
H5736.origine: The Hebrew verb adaph comes from a root that evokes the idea of overflowing or surpassing. The form used in the Bible is primarily the Qal (simple active form), which describes the state or action of being in excess. The Hiphil (causative form) would mean "to cause to have a surplus." This word belongs to the common vocabulary of the Old Testament to express anything that exceeds the measure or that remains after a sharing.
H5736.emploi: The verb adaph appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Exodus and Leviticus. It is used in concrete contexts of distribution (the manna in the desert), of measures and dimensions (the curtains of the tabernacle), and of accounts or transactions (the redemption of the firstborn, the sale of property). The word remains very practical and literal: it never designates something abstract, but always a measurable quantity. Its meaning varies slightly according to the context: "surplus" when it concerns what is kept or what remains, "to exceed" when comparing two numbers.
H5736.portee: This word reminds us how God provides exactly for needs: with the manna, there was neither surplus nor lack, everyone had what they needed (Exodus 16:18). It is an invitation to trust in divine providence rather than accumulating out of fear. It also shows that in God's order (the tabernacle, exchanges according to the Law), everything is measured and has nothing superfluous: every detail counts.

sens: Willing to act with zeal and determination
Equipped and prepared for battle
Resolved and willing in the fulfillment of a task
H5737A.detail:
1. The word describes an inner disposition of the soul: to be ready means having the heart turned toward action, a fervent desire to accomplish a task. It is not just being capable, but being animated by a sincere desire and determination. In 1 Chronicles 12:33, the men of Zebulun are "ready to go to battle with a resolute heart": their heart and will move in unison toward the fight.
2. The word includes the idea of being equipped and materially prepared: warriors are not only motivated, they are "armed" with all the necessary weapons and resources for combat. A ready soldier is a soldier who has what he needs at hand.
3. It also expresses unanimity and sincerity of heart: in 1 Chronicles 12:38, all these men arrive "ready to fight" and "with sincerity of heart." To be ready, therefore, also means to be in full agreement with all one's heart, without reservation or ulterior motives, in a communion of will with others.
H5737A.origine: The Hebrew verb עָדַר (adar) literally means to be ardent, to be awake, to have the heart turned toward something. It paints the image of a will that is animated and stands up. This verb expresses the idea of being prompt, zealous, mobilized internally — it is the heart that prepares before the hand and the weapon.
H5737A.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the military and political context of 1 Chronicles 12. It describes the warriors who gather around David to proclaim him king: in 12:33, the warriors of Zebulun are ready for battle with a resolute heart; in 12:38, all the fighters arrive at Hebron "ready to fight" and "with sincerity of heart." In these two uses, the word emphasizes not only military competence but especially emotional and spiritual commitment: these men do not fight out of obligation, but by a decision of the heart, a true communion of will around their leader.
H5737A.portee: This word reminds the reader that the true strength of a community (military, spiritual, or Christian) does not reside only in equipment or organization, but in the unity of heart and sincerity of commitment. To be "ready" is to give not only one's strength but also one's heart. For a Christian, this invites examination of whether he follows God's calls with that same sincere heart resolution, or if he obeys out of habit or obligation.

sens: To work the land with a pointed tool to turn it over and loosen it
To cultivate, maintain a field or vineyard
To leave abandoned, to cease cultivating
H5737B.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of turning the soil with a spade or pointed tool to prepare it for sowing seeds. It is a fundamental manual task in agriculture: the tool is driven into the ground and lifted to break clods and loosen the soil (Isaiah 7:25).
2. More broadly, it means to regularly maintain a field or vineyard through this plowing. It is the patient work of the farmer who cultivates his land and takes care of it. It is the opposite of abandonment: a spade-cultivated land is a living, productive land.
3. In contrast, the word also evokes the absence of cultivation, abandonment. When God says that a vineyard will no longer be "cultivated," He announces that it will return to a wild state, that thorns and brambles will take it over (Isaiah 5:6).
H5737B.origine: The Hebrew word עָדַר comes from a root that expresses the action of digging, turning over, loosening. It is related to the image of plowing: driving and lifting the tool in hard soil. It is a very concrete word, rooted in the agricultural life of the ancient Near East, where the spade and plowing were visible signs of care given to the land.
H5737B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in Isaiah, and both times in the passive form: "to be cultivated." In Isaiah 5:6, it describes a vineyard that God threatens to leave fallow, no longer cultivating or spading it: this will be the sign of His curse. In Isaiah 7:25, it refers to mountains that were once cultivated with a spade but will no longer be frequented because of the thorns. It is always in a context of judgment or misfortune: the cessation of plowing signals loss, abandonment, desolation.
H5737B.portee: This word reminds us that cultivating the land is hard, regular work that requires patience and care. Spiritually, it invites the believer to reflect on what he "cultivates" in his life: what areas of his heart or faith does he maintain, and which does he abandon to rust and thorns? It also raises the question of God's judgment: when He withdraws, He no longer "spades," allowing desolation to grow.

sens: To not be present, to be missing
To be absent from a group or assembly
To leave something without provision, to not meet a need
To disappear, to vanish
H5737C.detail:
1. The primary meaning is absence: something or someone is not where it should be. In 1 Samuel 30:19, none of David's captives "lacked" — they all returned with him, none had disappeared.
2. This also applies to the physical absence of a person from a group. In 2 Samuel 17:22, all of David's men crossed the Jordan, and "not one had stayed behind": no one was missing from the call.
3. The verb also denotes the action of not providing, of leaving without necessity. In 1 Kings 4:27, the stewards of King Solomon "did not let anything be lacking" at his table: they ensured complete provision for the king and his guests each month.
4. Finally, it means to disappear or vanish. In Isaiah 59:15, truth "has disappeared" from the earth — it has vanished because injustice reigns.
5. Applied to God's creatures, the verb expresses that nothing is lacking in the cosmic order. In Isaiah 40:26, none of the stars in the sky "is lacking": all are there, called by their name, under God's power.
H5737C.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of lack or absence. The most common form in the Bible is the Niphal (passive or reflexive form), which describes the state of what is lacking or missing. The same root gives related words denoting lack, absence, emptiness — everything that is not in its place.
H5737C.emploi: The verb "adhar" is infrequent in the Bible (7 occurrences). It mainly appears in narrative passages (1 and 2 Samuel) and in prophetic oracles (Isaiah). In its literal sense, it expresses physical absence: the warriors do not lack for David, no one is left out. In a figurative or cosmic sense, it expresses absence or lack of an established order: God's creatures do not lack their place, while human virtues (truth, righteousness) disappear when sin dominates. The context shows a contrast: on one side, the divine integrity that suffers no breach, on the other, the collapse of human order.
H5737C.portee: This word reminds us that God's faithfulness is absolute: none of His creatures are missing from the call, none of His promises fail. For the believer, this is a comfort: he can count on God without fear. In contrast, the absence of truth and righteousness in Isaiah 59:15 is a warning: when man strays from justice, everything collapses. It is an invitation to seek in God alone what cannot be lacking.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Beriah
Chief of the inhabitants of Ajalon
Brother of Arad, Ahio, and other Benjamites
H5738.detail:
1. Eder is a Benjamite, meaning a man who belongs to the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is the son of Beriah, as indicated in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8:15.
2. He is presented as a chief or important man among the inhabitants of Ajalon, a city in the region of Benjamin. His authority over this city shows that he held a position of responsibility within the community.
3. Eder is one of the eight sons of Beriah, alongside Arad, Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Mikha'el, and Joha. This large sibling group underscores the importance of family in the tribe of Benjamin.
H5738.origine: The name Eder literally means "flock" in Hebrew, evoking the image of a group of animals or a community. This name, like many Hebrew names, may reflect either a circumstance of birth or a desired quality for the child. The genealogical context shows that Eder lived during the time of the stay in Egypt and the desert, although he is mentioned late, only in the historical chronicles.
H5738.emploi: Eder appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:15, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. This passage enumerates the sons of Beriah, among whom Eder is named. There is no other mention of this man in the biblical texts, which means we know nothing else about his life or actions. His presence in this genealogy indicates only that he was a recognized ancestor of the Benjamites and that he held a position significant enough to be noted in the genealogical records.

sens: A group of domesticated animals, especially sheep and goats, that graze and move together
Collectively, the livestock of a region or property
Image of the people guided by God as a shepherd guides his flock
Figure of hair, eyes, or other features compared to the beauty of a flock
H5739.detail:
1. A flock is a group of domesticated animals that live and graze together under the care of a shepherd. In Genesis 29:2-3, Jacob finds "three flocks of sheep" resting near a well, which shows how livestock was kept in groups in the ancient Near East.
2. The term also refers to the entirety of a person's or region's livestock — the sum of their wealth. In 2 Chronicles 32:28, it is noted that King Hezekiah made flocks to show his abundance and prosperity.
3. The Bible uses the image of the flock to speak of the people of Israel guided by God. In Psalms 78:52, God "led his people like sheep" and "guided them like a flock in the wilderness" — expressing divine tenderness and constant direction.
4. In the love poems of the Song of Songs, the beloved's hair is compared to "a flock of goats" (6:5), an image of beauty and grace in the biblical poetic universe.
H5739.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of gathering and continuity. In biblical language, the flock represents much more than a mere collection of animals: it is an economic, social, and symbolic unit. The root is related to the idea of what stands together, what endures. The word appears regularly in texts where livestock is a primary measure of wealth, notably among the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) and in the pastoral contexts of the Near East.
H5739.emploi: The word "flock" appears 33 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the narratives of Genesis (where Jacob and Esau manage flocks), in the Psalms and the prophets, and in the Song of Songs. Its use varies according to context: in Genesis, it is concrete and economic (Genesis 29:2, 32:19); in the Psalms and among the prophets, it becomes metaphorical and theological to designate the people (Psalms 78:52; Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 31:10); in the Song of Songs, it enters lyrical poetry to evoke beauty (Song of Songs 4:1-2, 6:5-6). The nuance remains consistent: a directed, vulnerable group that needs a shepherd.
H5739.portee: Understanding that the Bible uses the flock to speak of our own relationship with God: we are the people He guides as a shepherd guides his flock, with tenderness and vigilance. This image reminds us that we are never left to ourselves, but are constantly under the care of the Lord. It also invites trust, for a shepherd watches over each sheep of his flock.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Merari during the time of King David
H5740A.detail:
1. Eder is a Levite of the tribe of Merari, mentioned during the time of King David and his organization of worship. He is the son of Muschi and the brother of Machli and Jeremoth (1 Chronicles 23:23). He appears in the lists of Levitical families responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple.
2. Eder is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in the first book of Chronicles in chapters 23 and 24, where King David organizes the Levitical services. These two passages provide the same information: Eder is among the sons of Muschi, belonging to the Merarite branch of the Levites. His name is included in the genealogical records intended to structure the temple's cultic ministry.
H5740A.origine: The name Eder means "a flock" in Hebrew, a common pastoral image in biblical culture. The meaning of the name perhaps evokes the notion of guarding or leading a group, which suited the Levites who cared for the affairs of the people and worship.
H5740A.emploi: Eder is mentioned only twice in the Bible. He is first mentioned during his marriage to Merab (1 Samuel 18:19), a marriage that is an important political and dynastic event: King Saul gives his daughter to Eder instead of giving her to David, marking a diversion from the promise made to the future king. He is then cited in the list of the five sons that Merab bore him (2 Samuel 21:8), in the context of a famine and judicial measures taken by David. These two mentions place him at the heart of the tensions between Saul and David.

sens: City in the southern part of Judah, at the border of Edom
H5740B.detail: Eder is a locality mentioned in the list of the southernmost cities of the territory of Judah. It is located at the southern edge of the tribe, near the border with Edom, the neighboring kingdom to the southeast. Its Hebrew name literally means "a flock," perhaps evoking a pastoral region or a place of livestock.
H5740B.origine: The Hebrew name עֵדֶר (eder) means "flock," "herd of animals." This root appears in other biblical contexts to designate groups of animals. The choice of this name for a city in southern Judah suggests that this region was characterized by pastoral farming.
H5740B.emploi: Eder appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:21, where it is listed among the cities enumerated in the extreme southern portion of the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah. This enumeration is part of the description of the borders and territorial possessions after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Man from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
Son of Barzillai
Husband of Merab, daughter of King Saul
H5741.detail:
1. Adriel is a man living during the time of King Saul and David, contemporary with the beginnings of the monarchy in Israel (1 Samuel 18:19).
2. He is the son of Barzillai, a man apparently of high social rank, as his lineage is mentioned in important genealogies (2 Samuel 21:8).
3. Adriel married Merab, the eldest daughter of King Saul, although the king had previously promised her hand to David (1 Samuel 18:19). Through this marriage, he entered the royal family.
H5741.origine: The name Adriel means "flock of God": it combines two Hebrew elements evoking the notion of flock (people) and divine belonging. It is a theophoric name, that is, bearing the name of God, which was common in Israel.
H5741.emploi: Adriel appears only twice in the Bible. He is first mentioned during his marriage to Merab (1 Samuel 18:19), a marriage that is an important political and dynastic event: King Saul gives his daughter to Adriel instead of to David, marking a diversion from the promise made to the future king. He is then cited in the list of the five sons that Merab bore him (2 Samuel 21:8), in the context of a famine and judicial measures taken by David. These two mentions place him at the heart of the tensions between Saul and David.

sens: round and flat dry legume, variable in color, that grows in pods
nutritious cheap food common in the ancient Near East
field or land cultivated where lentils grow
H5742.detail:
1. The lentil is a plant that produces small round and flattened seeds, resembling tiny coins. They are dried and boiled to make a nourishing stew. Jacob offers one to Esau to convince him to sell his birthright (Genesis 25:34).
2. This economical and fortifying food was also common on the tables of both the rich and the poor in Israel. David received some during his flight: the text lists what was brought to him, including lentils (2 Samuel 17:28).
3. By extension, the term "lentils" refers to the field or land where this crop grows. Shammah, a warrior of David, fought there alone against the Philistines without retreating, while the people fled (2 Samuel 23:11).
H5742.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that designates this particular legume, well attested in the ancient Levant. The lentil was one of the staples of the Mediterranean and Near Eastern diet, easy to cultivate, preserve, and transform into nutritious food.
H5742.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate the vegetable or the field. Three times it is mentioned as food: in the episode of Esau selling his birthright for a bowl of lentils (Genesis 25:34), in the list of provisions brought to David (2 Samuel 17:28), and in the recipe for famine bread prescribed to the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 4:9). Once, it is the field itself that is mentioned, during Shammah's battle (2 Samuel 23:11). The use remains purely referential and material.
H5742.portee: The lentil symbolizes in the Bible the ordinary, the humble, what is cheap — and this makes Esau's act even more serious, as he sacrifices a precious blessing to satisfy an immediate need. This detail invites the Christian reader to reflect on the difference between what nourishes the body for a day and what engages the whole life.

sens: Cover, envelop with a veil of clouds
Make dark, remove clarity
Hide, conceal from view by an obstruction
Figuratively: veil, disguise splendor or kindness
H5743.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of covering something with clouds: the Lord envelops the daughter of Zion under a thick cloud veil, as if the heavens darkened above her (Lamentations 2:1).
2. This covering creates darkness: light disappears, the day becomes twilight, everything becomes gray and oppressive.
3. The image suggests concealment: what was visible becomes hidden, what once radiated is now veiled — here, the magnificence of Israel, its glory, its luminous presence.
4. Figuratively, the cloud represents divine abandonment, the anger that hides the face of God: the once radiant nation is plunged into the darkness of divine discipline.
H5743.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of veiling or covering. The word עָב (ab) means "cloud" or "thick vapor." Here, the form used is the intensive (Hiphil), which reinforces the action: not only do clouds appear, but God causes them to intervene, placing them like a curtain. The image of the cloud is often that of divine presence, but also, in certain contexts of judgment, that of darkness and separation.
H5743.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 2:1, in a context of great distress. Jeremiah describes how God, in His anger against Jerusalem, covered the daughter of Zion with clouds — that is, He cast darkness over the city and its people. The context is that of the ruin of the temple and exile: the clouds do not bring life-giving rain, but judgment and apparent abandonment. It is a biblical hapax, a rare word, which underscores the intensity and uniqueness of this catastrophe.
H5743.portee: This word reminds the reader that spiritual and national crises can give the impression that God has hidden His face and favor. Yet, even under the clouds of judgment, faith learns that God will not be absent forever. Lamentations itself, despite its tone of distress, affirms that the compassion of the Lord has not ended (Lamentations 3:22), which encourages the Christian to persevere in trust, even in apparent darkness.

sens: son of Boaz and Ruth, grandfather of David
H5744G.detail: Obed is the son born from the union of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17). The neighbors of Naomi give him this name, recognizing that this child is a support and a blessing for his grandmother. Obed becomes the father of Jesse, who is himself the father of King David (Ruth 4:21-22). This is why Obed holds an important place in the genealogy of the Messiah: he embodies the link between the promise made to Judah and the fulfillment of that promise in David. His name means "servant" or "one who serves," which fits his role as a link in the chain of divine providence.
H5744G.origine: The Hebrew name Obed (עוֹבֵד) comes from the root "avad" which means "to serve" or "to work." It is a meaningful name that expresses the idea of service and dedication. In the Old Testament, names often carried a significance that reflected the circumstances of birth or the parents' expectations. The name Obed fits perfectly in the context of Ruth 4, where he is presented as one who will restore life to Naomi and serve God's plan.
H5744G.emploi: Obed appears in the Bible under five mentions, all related to his genealogy. He is first mentioned in Ruth 4:17, where the neighbors of Naomi give him this name at his birth, announcing that he will be a support for his grandmother. The following verses (Ruth 4:21-22) place him in the royal lineage: Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, Jesse fathered David. This same genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles 2:12. Obed does not intervene anywhere as an active character in the biblical narrative: he is mentioned only to show how the God of Israel led the lineage of Judah to messianic royalty. The Bible presents him mainly as a link in the chain of Providence.
H5744G.portee: Obed is a powerful reminder that God's hand works through ordinary generations and human situations. Through his existence, the biblical text shows how God can transform a situation of widowhood and poverty (that of Ruth and Naomi) into lasting blessing for an entire people. Obed is the ancestor of David, king of Israel, and thus the ancestor of the Messiah. The Christian reading this name understands that God does not disdain small things or marginalized people: it is in daily faithfulness and humble service that He accomplishes His greatest designs.

sens: Descendant of Jarha and Ephlal in the genealogy of Jerahmeel
H5744H.detail: 1. Obed is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jerahmeel. He is the son of Ephlal and the father of Jehu, in a lineage that traces back to Jarha, an Egyptian slave who became free through his marriage to the daughter of Sheshan (1 Chronicles 2:37-38).
H5744H.origine: The name Obed means "servant" in Hebrew, coming from the root עבד ("to serve"). It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several men of Judah at different times. The name reflects the idea of service, particularly relevant here since Obed appears in a lineage stemming from a former Egyptian servant who became a man of Judah.
H5744H.emploi: Obed appears twice in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 2, in verses 37 and 38. He is an ordinary man of Judah, known only by his place in the descent of Jerahmeel, one of the sons of Segub. Unlike another Obed in the Old Testament (grandfather of David), this one is identified only by his genealogical position as the son of Ephlal and father of Jehu.

sens: Elite soldier of King David
H5744I.detail: Obed is one of the valiant warriors listed among the "mighty men" of King David. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:47, amidst a list of fighters renowned for their courage and military strength in the service of the king.
H5744I.origine: The name Obed means "servant" or "one who serves" in Hebrew (from the root עבד, "to serve"). It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several different characters. Here, it designates a warrior attached to the service of King David.
H5744I.emploi: Obed appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:47. He is listed among thirty-two prestigious warriors recruited by David, all known for their exceptional valor. These "mighty men of David" formed an elite guard for the king and participated in Israel's great military campaigns. His appearance in this enumeration shows his rank and esteem at the royal court, although the Bible provides no details about his particular exploits.

sens: a Levite, son of Shemaiah, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H5744J.detail: Obed is a man of the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He was the son of Shemaiah and lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the north and the south. According to 1 Chronicles 26:7, he belonged to a family of warrior brothers, alongside his brothers Othni, Rephael, Elzabad, Elihu, and Shemaiah, suggesting that they were men of valor and likely servants of the temple or royal court.
H5744J.origine: The name Obed literally means "servant" or "one who serves," derived from the Hebrew root expressing the idea of servitude or service. It is a name that reflects the commitment of the people of Israel to serve God and fulfill religious or civil duties. Several characters bear this name in the Bible, including Obed son of Boaz and Ruth, ancestor of David, but this one is specifically identified as the son of Shemaiah.
H5744J.emploi: Obed appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:7, where he is listed among the sons of Shemaiah. This verse enumerates a family of valiant warrior brothers ("mighty men"), indicating that they likely held important positions, perhaps as temple guards or servants of the court. His appearance in this genealogy, during the time of the divided monarchy, shows that he was a member of a notable Levitical family that maintained the heritage of religious and military service in Israel.

sens: father of Azariah, Judean captain
man of God during the divided monarchy
H5744K.detail:
1. Obed is a Judean man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel (after the kingdom split into two). He is known as the father of Azariah, who becomes a military captain (chief of hundreds) in Judah.
2. His son Azariah plays an important role in the history of Judah: he participates in the revolt against Queen Athaliah by allying with the priest Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 23:1). Therefore, Obed belongs to a family of religious and military leaders of his time.
H5744K.origine: The name Obed means "servant" or "one who serves." It comes from the Hebrew root abad, which expresses the idea of serving, obeying, working for someone. This name reflects a posture of humility and dedication to God or to an established authority.
H5744K.emploi: Obed is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 23:1, where he is presented as the father of Azariah. In this passage, he is encountered in the context of a crucial political and religious revolt: that of Jehoiada the priest and his military allies against Queen Athaliah, who reigned in idolatry and violence. His son Azariah is one of the chief captains. This brief passage shows Obed as a member of a lineage of Judean leaders faithful to the interests of the kingdom and the faith.
H5744K.portee: The name Obed reminds us that even lesser-known or less-mentioned biblical figures are part of a larger story of obedience and service. His son participates in a decisive moment when the Judean people rise up against impiety. This shows that faithful actions, even in the shadows, contribute to God's purpose in the history of His people.

sens: Son of Joktan, ancestor of a pre-flood Arab tribe
H5745.detail: Obal is a biblical character mentioned only once in the genealogy of the descendants of Shem. He is the son of Joktan and is part of the list of twelve sons of Joktan, listed in Genesis 10:28 alongside his brothers Abimael and Sheba. According to tradition, Obal was the founder of an Arab tribe.
H5745.origine: The name Obal, in Hebrew עוֹבָל, literally means "stripped bare" or "made bare." This image of nakedness may evoke circumstances of his time or lineage. The name also exists in the alternative form עֵיבָל (Ebal) in some manuscripts, showing variations in the transmission of the Hebrew text.
H5745.emploi: Obal appears exclusively in the genealogy of Genesis 10, which lists the peoples descended from the three sons of Noah after the Flood. This account classifies Obal among the descendants of Shem through Joktan, placing him in the history of Semitic and Arab peoples. His insertion in this genealogical list suggests that he founded or gave his name to a people or a region of the Arab world, even though the Bible does not further develop his story.

sens: Prepare food over fire, especially bread or cakes
Cook something by subjecting it to heat
H5746.detail:
1. Prepare food over fire, particularly bread or cakes. In Ezekiel 4:12, the prophet is to bake barley cakes using impure fuel: this is the concrete action of subjecting the dough to heat to transform it into food.
2. The verb denotes the act of cooking, transforming by heat. It is a mundane culinary gesture in itself, but it becomes dramatic and symbolic in the context of Ezekiel's vision: the ordinary of the household becomes a sign of dishonor and judgment.
H5746.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of cooking over fire. It is a simple verb from the everyday vocabulary of domestic life, particularly related to the preparation of bread, a fundamental food in ancient diets. The family of the word includes the name that designates the oven.
H5746.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 4:12. It is in a prophetic vision where God commands the prophet to bake barley bread with forbidden fuel (human excrement), to symbolize the impurity and defeat of Israel during the siege of Jerusalem. The ordinary culinary action becomes a prophetic and symbolic act, illustrating the humiliation of the people.
H5746.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of concrete life — food, home, daily gestures — and that it can transform ordinary acts into powerful symbols of God's judgment or grace. The context of Ezekiel shows how indignity reaches even into the intimacy of the home and the table.

sens: king of the Amorites who ruled over Bashan at the time of the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan
giant of the Rephaim race
adversary defeated by Moses and the Israelites at Edrei
H5747.detail:
1. Og was an Amorite king (from the people of the Amorites) who controlled the territory of Bashan, east of the Jordan, at the time when Israel was leaving Egypt and entering Canaan. His name literally means "long-necked," which evokes his imposing nature. He is first mentioned in Numbers 21:33, when he comes out to meet Israel with his entire army to fight.
2. Og belonged to the ancient race of the Rephaim, giants known for their great size. Joshua 13:12 describes him as "the only remnant of the Rephaim," emphasizing that he was one of the last representatives of this formidable race. His exceptional stature made him a feared adversary.
3. Moses and Israel defeated Og in the battle of Edrei (Deuteronomy 3:1-3), killing him and all his people and taking possession of his kingdom. This victory over a giant demonstrates the power that the Lord granted to Israel and remains a memorable reminder of His protection: Psalm 136:20 celebrates "him who struck down Og, king of Bashan."
H5747.origine: The name "Og" probably means "long-necked" in ancient Hebrew, a description that may reflect his stature as a giant. It was a title or nickname characteristic of an impressive leader. The historical figure remains anchored in biblical memory as a symbol of the earthly power that God had subjected to Israel during the conquest.
H5747.emploi: Og appears in 22 biblical passages, mainly in the books of Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua, where he embodies the major adversary against Israel during the Exodus and the conquest of the Jordan. The historical books (Kings) and the Psalms also mention him as a memorable example of divine victory. The account of his defeat is reported twice (Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3), highlighting his importance. Og illustrates how God delivers powerful enemy kings to Israel, even giants: this victory becomes a motif of praise in the Psalms (135:11 and 136:20).
H5747.portee: The victory over Og teaches the Christian people that God is more powerful than seemingly insurmountable obstacles: even a giant and an Amorite king cannot resist Him who walks with His people. It shows that the most formidable challenges, without faith in the Lord, are fragile before His hand.

sens: Wind instrument made of reed or wood, capable of producing musical sounds
Sound produced by this instrument
Musical expression of joy or rejoicing
Expression of sadness or lamentation
H5748.detail: 1. The chalumeau is a wind instrument, probably made of reed or wood, that is played by blowing into it to produce sounds (Genesis 4:21 mentions it among the first instruments created by man). 2. By extension, the word refers to the sounds produced by this instrument — a characteristic tone that fills a space or rises into the air (Job 21:12 associates it with the tambourine and harp to express rejoicing). 3. In the context of praise and celebration, the chalumeau represents a voice of joy: along with other instruments, it is offered to God in an act of worship (Psalms 150:4 invites it to participate in divine praise). 4. The same instrument can express mourning and lament — when Job speaks of his chalumeau that produces only plaintive sounds, he evokes a broken voice, transformed by suffering (Job 30:31).
H5748.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of blowing or creating a sound. It is a popular instrument in the ancient Near East, also attested in neighboring cultures. The chalumeau belongs to the family of primitive wind instruments, capable of modulating different tones depending on the musician's technique.
H5748.emploi: The chalumeau appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a musical and festive or painful context. Genesis 4:21 associates it with Jubal, the ancestor of musicians, giving it a prestigious place in the origins of human music. In Job, it appears twice: once in the scene of the rejoicing of the wicked (Job 21:12), and once in the expression of Job's own distress (Job 30:31), showing that the same instrument can express contrary emotions depending on who plays it and their state of mind. Finally, Psalms 150:4 invites it to divine praise, alongside other instruments. The chalumeau is always linked to a strong collective or personal dimension: it is played to celebrate or to mourn.
H5748.portee: The chalumeau reminds us that music is a divine gift, inscribed in human history from its origins. This instrument also shows that joy and sadness are expressed through the same means: it is the state of the heart that transforms a sound into a cry of celebration or lamentation. For the believer, seeing the chalumeau invited to praise God (Psalms 150:4) means that everything given to us for expression should be able to glorify our Creator.

sens: To keep standing, to prevent from falling
To surround, to encircle
To strengthen, to lift up in difficulty
To persevere, to hold firm
H5749A.detail:
1. To keep standing, to prevent from falling: the verb evokes the action of holding someone or something that is at risk of collapsing. In Psalms 20:9, "we stand firm" means to remain standing and stable in the face of threat.
2. To surround, to encircle: the image is that of a presence that envelops from all sides. In Psalms 119:61, the traps of the wicked "surround me," meaning they encircle me like a belt of danger.
3. To strengthen, to lift up in difficulty: this means helping someone who is weak or overwhelmed to regain their strength. In Psalms 146:9, the Lord "supports the orphan and the widow," meaning He protects them and lifts them from their distress. Similarly, in Psalms 147:6, He "supports the downtrodden."
4. To persevere, to hold firm: the word can also express the ability to remain morally and spiritually upright despite trials, as in Psalms 20:9 where the people "stand firm."
H5749A.origine: The Hebrew verb עוּד comes from a root that evokes the idea of standing upright, returning, repeating, or doing again. Depending on the grammatical context (Piel, Pilel, or Hithpalel forms), the meaning nuances: it can mean "to surround" (repeated action around), "to lift up," or "to be lifted up." The basic image is that of stability and circular movement or returning to a standing position.
H5749A.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Segond in the Psalms, always in a poetic and spiritual register. In Psalms 20:9, it expresses the firmness of the people who "stand firm." In Psalms 119:61, it describes the threatening encirclement of traps. But the dominant usage is that of divine support: in Psalms 146:9 and 147:6, the Lord "supports" (or "lifts up") the weak and the downtrodden. The word thus focuses on two ideas: physical or moral stability, and God's protective and strengthening action towards the fragile.
H5749A.portee: This word reveals that human stability is not natural: we risk falling, being encircled by evil, being crushed by trials. But it invites us to recognize that God is the one who "supports" — who lifts up the orphans, the widows, the downtrodden. It is a call to trust not in our own strength, but in the faithful support of the Lord who does not let His own fall.

sens: To attest something solemnly and repeatedly
To cite someone as a witness, to invoke their presence to confirm a word
To warn insistently, to caution
To blame, to reproach, to urge someone to return
To make an official statement before judges or witnesses
H5749B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to attest something forcefully and solemnly, often by repeating it: it is to bear witness, to affirm the truth of a word or fact. When Jeremiah receives the order to speak to the people, he testifies against them on behalf of God (Jeremiah 11:7).
2. This verb is used to take someone as a witness, meaning to publicly invoke them to confirm what is said or to be a guarantor. Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses to the choice he presents to the Israelites (Deuteronomy 30:19).
3. The word also designates the act of warning seriously and insistently, of cautioning: King Solomon warns Shimei that if he leaves Jerusalem, he will die (1 Kings 2:42).
4. To testify can also mean to blame or reproach energetically, to urge someone to change their behavior: the prophets urged the people to return to God, but they rebelled (Nehemiah 9:26).
5. In a judicial context, it means to make a deposition before judges: two men testify against Naboth saying that he has cursed God and the king (1 Kings 21:10).
H5749B.origine: This verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of repetition and firmness. The word appears mainly in the reinforced form (the equivalent of Hiphil in Hebrew), which adds to the basic idea a sense of solemnity and urgency. The root itself evokes the act of saying something again, insistently, as if to make it better understood and accepted. This is why the verb is suitable for both attestation and warning.
H5749B.emploi: This verb appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Nehemiah) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Malachi, Amos). It is particularly frequent in Deuteronomy, where Moses testifies and warns Israel to keep the covenant. The verb slightly changes nuance depending on the context: it can mean "to warn" when it is about cautioning (Nehemiah 13:21), "to testify" when calling a witness to confirm something (Deuteronomy 30:19), or "to urge" when a prophet exhorts the people with urgency (Nehemiah 9:26). In legal contexts, it designates the deposition of a witness (1 Kings 21:10). It is a key word to express the urgency and authority with which God, through His prophets and servants, calls His people to obey.
H5749B.portee: This word shows how seriously God takes the relationship He has established with His people: He does not merely give orders, He testifies, He warns, He urges the people to return to Him. It is a language that expresses both love (the urgency to save) and authority. For the reader, this verb invites us to listen to God's warnings with the same seriousness: when He speaks, it is never a light word, it is a word that imposes itself with force. It is also a call not to ignore divine warnings, for they always aim for the good of the people.

sens: What persists, continues
What adds, repeats
What comes after, again
Beyond, in addition, elsewhere
H5750.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the continuation, the persistence of an action or state: Adam "still" knows his wife and she gives birth again (Genesis 4:25), meaning he continues to live with her. This conveys the sense of duration that extends.
2. It also expresses addition or repetition: after a first battle, there is "still" a battle at Gob (2 Samuel 21:18), meaning an additional battle. One thing is added to what was already there.
3. It signifies "again," marking the return of an action or situation: Jeremiah cries that there is "no one to pitch his tent again" (Jeremiah 10:20), meaning to restore it after its destruction.
4. It also carries the meaning of "more," "furthermore," or "in addition": the servant will serve "no longer" after fifty years (Numbers 8:25), the speaker will be "no longer" mute (Ezekiel 24:27). It is the word of surpassing or changing state.
H5750.origine: The Hebrew word עוֹד comes from a root that expresses the idea of continuous movement, circulation, of what persists over time. Its primary image is that of something that "turns round," that continues: this is why it can mean "continuance" or "perseverance." In Aramaic, the same word עוֹד is found with the same meaning of persistence. The central notion is that of time extending or an action prolonging beyond the moment it is stated.
H5750.emploi: This word appears 461 times in the Old Testament, particularly frequent in Genesis and in the historical books. It is used sometimes as an adverb of continuation ("as long as," "for as long as"), sometimes as an adverb of addition ("another son," "another battle"), and sometimes to mark the negation of continuation ("no longer"). In the accounts of Abraham and Jacob, for example, it expresses the expectation and repetition of divine promises. In prophetic passages like Jeremiah or Ezekiel, it marks the turning point, the change from an old situation to a new one. It is a very flexible word, adapting to the nuances of the context: it can express hope (continuation of life), concern (addition of troubles), or assurance (God speaks "still").
H5750.portee: This small rich word teaches the reader that history is never truly finished in God's eyes. Promises continue ("still"), trials may return ("still"), but grace also renews. For the one who reads the Bible, recognizing this word in Hebrew is to discover that nothing is definitive in human history except the word of God: it persists "still" when everything collapses.

sens: At the moment when
While
Still in the act of
H5751.detail:
1. This word marks that the action is unfolding at the moment when something else occurs. In Daniel 4:31, Nebuchadnezzar speaks his words when a voice from heaven suddenly sounds — the word was "still" in his mouth, meaning he was still speaking when the divine interruption came.

2. It also expresses the continuity of a situation: the action is not finished, it prolongs. The word emphasizes that the present moment has not marked the end of what is happening.
H5751.origine: In Aramaic (the language spoken in Daniel 4), this word comes from the same root as in Hebrew "od" (עוֹד) which literally means "continue, last." It is the same term as that in the Hebrew Old Testament, but here in its Aramaic form. The root evokes the idea of what subsists, of what is not yet finished.
H5751.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:31. At this moment in the narrative, King Nebuchadnezzar boasts of his exploits and power, proclaiming the wonders of Babylon. It is precisely "still" — while he speaks — that a heavenly voice intervenes to judge him and announce his downfall. The use of "still" creates a dramatic contrast: at the moment when the king reigns at his peak, God takes away his power.
H5751.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp how God intervenes in human history, often when least expected. Nebuchadnezzar is in full glory when the sentence falls: this shows that no one is assured of their power in the face of divine sovereignty. It is a lesson in humility about the fragility of human authority.

sens: father of the prophet Azaria during the reign of King Asa of Judah
prophet of the Lord in Samaria at the time of Pekah's invasion
H5752G.detail: 1. Obed is the father of Azaria, a prophet who received the Spirit of God and spoke to King Asa of Judah to encourage him to reform the kingdom (2 Chronicles 15:1). 2. Obed is also a prophet of the Lord who ministered in Samaria: he delivered a prophecy that strengthened King Asa and urged him to destroy the idols and restore the altar of the Lord in front of the porch of the temple (2 Chronicles 15:8).
H5752G.origine: The name Obed means "one who restores" or "servant." It expresses the idea of restoring, putting things in order. Two figures bear this name in the account of the divided kingdom: one is the father of a prophet, the other is herself a prophet and plays a role in spiritual restoration with the king.
H5752G.emploi: Obed appears twice in the Second Book of Chronicles, during the reign of King Asa of Judah (around 912-872 B.C.). First mentioned as the father of the prophet Azaria (2 Chronicles 15:1), he is then presented as a prophet from Samaria who confronted King Asa during Pekah's invasion of Israel. His prophecy and call to repentance had a decisive impact on the king's religious policy, leading him to destroy the idols and strengthen the worship of the Lord.
H5752G.portee: These two accounts of Obed illustrate how God raises up prophets to call His people to faithfulness and spiritual restoration. The ministry of Obed shows that the true strength of a king lies not in weapons, but in obedience to God and the rejection of idols. His call to Asa invites every believer to examine their heart and turn to God sincerely.

sens: prophet of the Lord in the Northern kingdom (Samaria)
man who intercedes for the captives and the oppressed
H5752H.detail: Oded is a prophet who lived in Samaria at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. When King Pekah's army returns from Judah with captives, Oded stands before them to confront them in the name of God (2 Chronicles 28:9). He is a man who dares to speak to the king and his soldiers, reproaching them for their excessive anger and urging them to show mercy: he encourages them to release the prisoners and send them back to their homes.
H5752H.origine: The name Oded means "restorer" or "one who straightens." It comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of restoring, lifting up what has fallen. This name suits the character well: he is a prophet who seeks to correct the conscience of a nation, striving to restore justice and compassion.
H5752H.emploi: Oded appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:9. He is a prophet from Samaria (the Northern kingdom) at the time when King Pekah of Israel has defeated King Ahaz of Judah and brings back captives. What is remarkable is that this prophet from the Northern kingdom intercedes for the inhabitants of the Southern kingdom, oppressed and mistreated. His action shows that even in the political chaos of division, God raises voices to remind His commandments: not to forget mercy.
H5752H.portee: Oded illustrates the role of the biblical prophet: not only to announce the Word of God, but also to intervene concretely to defend the weak and the captives. His courage to confront the victorious army invites the reader not to be swept away by vengeance or cruelty, even when one feels justified. It is a lesson in compassion amid political violence.

sens: To bend or curve something or someone strongly
To become bent, weakened, crushed
To distort, alter, or corrupt what is right and just
To deeply disturb or trouble
To act in a twisted, perverse manner
H5753A.detail:
