H5780I.detail: Uts is a personal name borne by at least one man in the genealogy of the Edomites. He appears in the list of descendants of Seir the Horite: he is the son of Dishan (or Eser according to some textual variants) and the brother of Aran. This genealogy appears twice in the Bible: in Genesis 36:28 and in 1 Chronicles 1:42, showing the importance given to the preservation of these Edomite lineages.
H5780I.origine: The name Uts means "wooded" or "covered with woods" in Hebrew. It is a name particular to the genealogies of the neighboring peoples of Israel, notably the Edomites, descendants of Esau.
H5780I.emploi: Uts appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists of Edomites. In Genesis 36:28, he is presented as the son of Dishan and brother of Aran in the lineage of Seir. The same genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:42, confirming this lineage. These references show that the name was used to establish kinship ties among the Canaanite peoples contemporary to Israel.

sens: Region located east and southeast of Palestine, in the Arabian desert
Homeland of Job, the righteous sufferer of the Old Testament
H5780J.detail:
1. Uts is a geographical region located east and southeast of Palestine, probably on the edge of the Arabian desert. It appears in biblical texts as a distant land, distinct from the land of Israel (Job 1:1).
2. Uts is best known as the land from which Job originated, this righteous man whom God tested with terrible sufferings. It is there that he lived at the beginning of his story and endured his misfortunes (Job 1:1). The mention of Uts situates Job's story outside of Israel, with a pious man who did not belong to the chosen people but served the true God.
H5780J.origine: The name Uts comes from the word that evokes the idea of forest or wooded region. This region is not clearly identified on modern maps, but it designates an area known to ancient Israelites as distant and at the edge of the civilized world, probably in northern Arabia or in territories situated between Mesopotamia and Palestine.
H5780J.emploi: Uts appears three times in the Bible. It is first mentioned as the setting of the book of Job (Job 1:1), establishing that the wise man was a non-Israelite but faithful to God. It is then cited among the nations called to drink the cup of divine wrath (Jeremiah 25:20), associated with Arabia and the Philistines, confirming its location on the periphery of the biblical world. Finally, it is mentioned in Lamentations (4:21) as an inhabited place, possibly identified with Edom or its surroundings. These three occurrences situate Uts as a real but distant territory, known to biblical prophets and historians.

sens: Exert strong pressure that crushes or destroys
Wear down, compact through repeated passage
Oppress, weigh down under a burden
H5781.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to crush by force: to apply a weight that grinds or destroys. In Amos 2:13, God says, "I will crush you as a cart crushes when loaded with sheaves" — the image of the heavily loaded cart sinking and compressing the ground perfectly illustrates this violent compression action.
2. The word can also describe the gradual wear of something trampled, pressed: a ground crushed by repeated passage, flattened and compacted.
3. In a figurative sense, to crush means to oppress or weigh down: to exert a crushing force on someone or something, reducing or annihilating it. In Amos 2:13, this is indeed the meaning: God threatens to overwhelm Israel under the weight of His judgment, just as a cart crushes the ground.
H5781.origine: The Hebrew root עוּק (uq) evokes the idea of pressure, compression, force exerted from above. The word belongs to the family of verbs of violent action. The form used here (the Hiphil) reinforces the meaning: it makes it active and intensive — "to cause to be crushed," "to bring about crushing."
H5781.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 2:13. The prophet Amos uses it in a word of judgment from God against Israel: the people have accumulated transgressions, and God declares that He will crush them. It is an image of divine threat, staging the contrast between God's omnipotence and the vulnerability of the people. The context (the cart loaded with sheaves) makes the image concrete and terrifying.
H5781.portee: This word reminds us of the warning that God addresses to His people: injustice, oppression, and disobedience have crushing consequences. For the Christian reading Amos, it is a call to take seriously divine justice and the holiness of God — not to live in fear, but to walk in respectful fear and obedience.

sens: To wake up, to come out of sleep
To be set in motion, stimulated
To incite someone to act, to push them to action
To excite, to kindle (a feeling, a force)
To bring forth, to cause to arise (a person, an event)
To show oneself active, to get moving
H5782.detail:
1. To wake up or wake someone from sleep: the most concrete meaning. In Song of Solomon 8:5, the beloved says, "I awakened you under the apple tree," evoking a waking to life and love.
2. To be awakened, set in action after inaction or forgetfulness: it is to move from immobility to liveliness. In Psalms 35:23, the psalmist cries, "Awake!" addressing God, urging Him to come out of His apparent silence.
3. To incite someone to act, to give them the impulse, the momentum: in Judges 5:12, Deborah is "awakened" so that she may rise and act. It is to stir up energy and will.
4. To excite, to kindle a feeling or a force: in Hosea 7:4, one "kindles" the fire of the oven, meaning to intensify it. Similarly, in Proverbs 10:12, hatred can "excite" quarrels.
5. To bring forth, to make a new person or event appear: in Isaiah 41:2, God "raises up" someone from the east, causing them to emerge as a new actor on the scene.
6. To show oneself active, to intervene with vigor: in Isaiah 51:9, the arm of the Lord is asked to awaken to act with power.
H5782.origine: The Hebrew verb עוּר (ur) comes from a root that expresses the idea of movement and vigilance: to come out of inertia, to take action. The family of the word includes forms that mark the intensity of action: from simple waking to lively excitement and movement. The primary image is that of eyes opening or a sleeper waking; it then extends to all forms of activation, whether physical, emotional, or moral.
H5782.emploi: This verb appears 65 times in the Old Testament, especially in Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, three books rich in prayers and prophetic messages. In Psalms, it often expresses the supplication addressed to God for Him to wake up and intervene on behalf of His people (Psalms 35:23, 44:24). In Isaiah, it describes God's action in raising up a deliverer (41:2, 41:25) or calling Jerusalem to rise from its exile (51:9, 52:1). In Jeremiah and Ezekiel, it marks the divine intervention that raises enemies against Judah. In the Song of Solomon, it takes on a tender and loving hue, with the beloved waking the one they love. The verb nuances according to the context: a call to wake up, a call to action, passionate incitement, or prophetic intervention.
H5782.portee: This word reminds us that the God of Israel is never asleep or indifferent: when His people cry out to Him, He awakens to act. It also invites everyone not to remain inert before God's calls, but to wake up and rise to serve Him. It is a word of hope: even when everything seems frozen or lost, God can bring forth liberation, cause deliverance to arise. For the Christian reader, it speaks of resurrection and new life: that of Christ rising from the tomb, that of the believer waking to faith.

sens: To be stripped of what covers, exposed to view
To be revealed, uncovered, with no possible secret
To be rendered powerless, emptied of strength
H5783.detail: 1. The verb evokes the action of stripping something of its covering or what protects it: the nakedness that results from unveiling. In Habakkuk 3:9, God's bow is "laid bare," meaning ready to act without obstacle, drawn and visible. 2. By extension, to be exposed means to be revealed, known, impossible to hide. Nothing can remain secret before God. 3. Finally, the image also evokes a form of vulnerability or defeat: the one who is laid bare finds themselves disarmed, without possible defense against the one who looks at them.
H5783.origine: This Hebrew root עור (ur) primarily denotes physical unveiling. The text of Habakkuk uses the word to speak of the "curses" that become manifest (the word that strikes), laid bare by divine power. It is a rare word in Hebrew, emphasizing sudden revelation and forced exposure.
H5783.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew (Habakkuk 3:9). It describes the Lord's bow made visible and ready, a symbol of His imminent judgment and fearsome word. The context is prophetic: Habakkuk sees the manifestation of God's power preparing to strike and transform the earth. The image of the bow laid bare underscores the irresistible and manifest nature of divine judgment.
H5783.portee: This word reminds us that nothing escapes the gaze and judgment of God: everything is or will be exposed before Him. For the believer, it is an invitation to honesty and sincerity in prayer and in life. It also evokes that God's power, though often hidden, will fully manifest at the appointed time.

sens: The lightweight husk of grain that separates from wheat or barley during threshing
That which is light, insubstantial, and easily carried away by the wind
That which is worthless, useless, destined to disappear
H5784.detail:
1. Chaff is the thin, dry covering that surrounds the grain of wheat or barley. During threshing, the good grain is separated from this lightweight covering. In Israel, the threshed sheaves were thrown into the air so that the wind would carry away the chaff while the grain fell back down: this is what Daniel 2:35 evokes when it describes the debris of the statue "like the chaff that blows away from a threshing floor in summer."
2. Because it is very light, chaff symbolizes everything that has no solidity and that the wind scatters effortlessly. In Daniel's vision, all the empires represented by iron, clay, and precious metals are reduced to debris without substance, carried away like chaff by a breath.
3. Metaphorically, chaff represents what is futile, without true value. In the face of the eternal mountain that the stone becomes (symbolizing the kingdom of God), all human kingdoms are but chaff: destined for complete oblivion, as if there is "no trace" left of what has disappeared.
H5784.origine: The Hebrew word עוּר (ur) literally means "husk" or "shell." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of being light, stripped. In biblical Hebrew, this term specifically designates the residues of threshing wheat, well-known in a Mediterranean agricultural culture.
H5784.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in the passage of Daniel 2:35. This verse uses chaff as an image to show the complete and definitive annihilation of human empires in the face of God's eternal reign. By comparing the debris of kingdoms to chaff carried away by the wind, the prophet emphasizes that despite their apparent power (represented by iron, gold, and silver), these empires have no spiritual substance and are destined to disappear without leaving a trace.
H5784.portee: This biblical image reminds the believer that all earthly greatness, all human power and wealth are fragile and temporary compared to the eternal kingdom of God. In the face of the challenges and powers of the world, the text invites us to place our trust, not in what is light like chaff, but in what endures: the government of the God who fills the whole earth.

sens: Body covering that protects the human or animal body
Material transformed into leather or fabric, used in worship or daily life
External aspect or visible appearance of a person
Expression of the body's vulnerability and suffering
H5785.detail:
1. The skin is the covering that protects the human body or that of animals. This is the simplest meaning: after sin, God makes garments of skin for Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:21), which implies having skinned animals. Leviticus dedicates a long passage to examining skin diseases and wounds to distinguish unclean leprosy from the rest (Leviticus 13:11).

2. The skin becomes raw material: it is worked into leather or fabric for the needs of worship or practical life. The ark is covered with skins of rams dyed red (Exodus 25:5), and the priest wears the skin of the offered victim (Leviticus 7:8). Elijah wears a leather belt (2 Kings 1:8), a symbol of strength and austere life.

3. The skin symbolizes the external appearance, what is seen of a person. Jacob puts goat skins on his arms so that his father confuses him with Esau (Genesis 27:16): he hides his true nature under a false appearance.

4. The skin also expresses bodily fragility and suffering. Job cries that his skin dries up and changes color due to illness (Job 7:5, Job 30:30), a universal experience of physical evil. That is why Job says: "skin for skin" — the idea that one sacrifices everything they have to keep their life (Job 2:4).
H5785.origine: The Hebrew word "or" (עוֹר) is ancient and fundamental. It first designates the living surface of the body that protects it from the outside world — the image of a fragile boundary between the inside and the outside. The word has changed little throughout history and has few variants: the language uses it as is to speak of raw skin or skin transformed into useful material. It is a very concrete term, linked to the sensory experience of the body and its fragilities.
H5785.emploi: The word "skin" appears 82 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Leviticus (chapters 13 and 15), where it concerns examining skin diseases for ritual purity. It also appears abundantly in Exodus for the materials of the Tabernacle, and is found in the narratives of Genesis (the first garments, Jacob's deception), in Job's poems about suffering, and in Lamentations about the distress of the besieged people. Each context nuances the meaning: the skin is primarily the living place of health or disease, then the dead material transformed into a resource, and finally the image of human fragility in the face of evil.
H5785.portee: Meditating on the skin brings us back to the reality of the body: the Bible is not spiritual at a distance from the flesh. God clothes the naked body of Adam and Eve; He establishes laws on skin diseases to protect community life; He sees Job's suffering written on every inch of sick skin. This teaches us that the body is not a contemptible prison, but the true substance of our existence, and that God cares about it.

sens: To gouge out the eyes, to take away sight physically
To deprive of discernment, to obscure judgment
H5786.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the act of gouging out the eyes or taking away someone's sight. It is a violent act of punishment: in Jeremiah 39:7, the king of Babylon has Zedekiah's eyes gouged out before deporting him in chains. It is a mutilation that renders the person completely dependent.
2. The word is also used figuratively to describe how something obscures judgment or distorts perception. In Exodus 23:8, gifts "blind those who have their eyes open": that is, corruption prevents even the wise from seeing justice. The word evokes a moral blindness, where reason and fairness disappear.
H5786.origine: The Hebrew verb עָוַר (a.var) literally means to make blind or without sight. Its root expresses the idea of darkness and deprivation of the sense of sight. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms concerning blindness and obscurity, and it describes both physical condition and spiritual or moral incapacity.
H5786.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, always in Hebrew. Three occurrences (2 Kings 25:7, Jeremiah 39:7, and 52:11) describe the same historical event: the gouging out of Zedekiah's eyes, the last king of Judah, by Nebuchadnezzar — an act of domination and massive humiliation. Two occurrences (Exodus 23:8 and Deuteronomy 16:19) use the word metaphorically to speak of the corruption of judges: bribes "blind" the eyes of the wise, rendering them incapable of seeing the truth.
H5786.portee: This word reminds Christians of the reality of sin in two areas: the destructive power of violence and tyranny, and the formidable capacity of corruption to paralyze moral judgment. The usages related to judges show that even the wisest can be "blinded" by self-interest — a warning against complacency in the realm of justice and integrity.

sens: One who cannot see, deprived of sight
One who lacks discernment or spiritual understanding
One who acts without clear vision, blindly
H5787.detail:
1. The word first describes one who is physically deprived of their eyes or the ability to see. In Exodus 4:11, God asserts that it is He who makes one "blind" or seeing; in Deuteronomy 15:21, a blind animal cannot be offered as a sacrifice, as it has a defect. It is a concrete infirmity, often associated with other disabilities like lameness (2 Samuel 5:6).
2. The word extends to one who does not understand, who lacks wisdom or spiritual insight. In Isaiah 42:19, the prophet reproaches Israel for being "blind" — not physically, but unable to discern God's will despite His signs. It is a blindness of the heart and spirit.
3. One who "blinds" acts without seeing where they are going, without wisdom. In Deuteronomy 27:18, cursing someone by making them "blind" (leading them astray) on the path is a crime; in Isaiah 59:10, Israel gropes like a blind person, meaning without direction or certainty.
H5787.origine: The Hebrew word עִוֵּר (ivver) comes from a root that literally means "without light on the eyes." It first designates the physical absence of vision. In Hebrew, the family of this word also includes the idea of confusion and loss of direction. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) translates it with the Greek τυφλός (typhlos), which captures exactly this same distinction between physical blindness and spiritual obscurity, very common among the prophets.
H5787.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and the Prophets (particularly Isaiah). In the Law, it describes physical infirmity and the duties towards those who suffer from it (not cursing them in Deuteronomy 27:18; respecting the blind in Leviticus 19:14). In the Psalms and the Prophets, "blind" becomes mainly an image: Isaiah prophesies that God will open the eyes of the blind (Isaiah 35:5, 42:7), which announces messianic healing. Isaiah also reproaches Israel for being blind to divine revelation (Isaiah 42:18-19). The word thus oscillates between the literal and the figurative, inviting us to see in physical blindness an image of spiritual wandering.
H5787.portee: This word teaches believers that God has compassion for the weak and suffering: He opens the eyes of the blind. It also calls us to spiritual vigilance: we can be "blind" without realizing it, unable to discern the truth if our hearts harden. Finally, it urges us to respect and serve those who suffer from a disability, knowing that no infirmity separates us from divine love.

sens: State of one who cannot see, who has lost sight
Mental confusion, wandering of the mind
Deprivation of moral or spiritual judgment
H5788A.detail:
1. Blindness is primarily the physical loss of sight: it is the inability to see. In Deuteronomy 28:28, God threatens to strike Israel with blindness among other plagues, like a disease or infirmity sent as punishment.
2. The word also denotes confusion of the mind, mental delirium: blindness then becomes a darkness that reigns in the head and heart. In Zechariah 12:4, it strikes the horses of the peoples—not their physical sight, but drives them mad, leads them astray, makes them useless in battle.
3. By extension, blindness means the inability to understand the truth, to discern good from evil. It is a state where one no longer sees clearly, spiritually or morally.
H5788A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be blind" or "obscured." It is the name that designates this state of absence of sight or clarity. The root evokes the idea of closure, darkness: one who cannot see is confined in darkness. The word appears in two forms in ancient Hebrew: this masculine form (עִוָּרוֹן) and a feminine form (עַוֶּרֶת), but they denote the same reality.
H5788A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 28:28, it is one of the punishments that God sends upon His unfaithful people—a concrete plague, among other diseases and calamities. In Zechariah 12:4, it strikes the enemies of Israel, the horses of the peoples who attack it, as a form of divine judgment: a confusion and disorientation that render them powerless. In both cases, blindness is a judgment, a consequence of rejecting God or hostility towards His people.
H5788A.portee: For the Bible reader, blindness serves as a reminder that far from God, man becomes spiritually blind—unable to see the truth, the good, the direction of God. It is a strong image of the consequences of sin and rejection of God: not only does one suffer an external punishment, but one also loses inner clarity. Conversely, God's promise in Zechariah to keep eyes open on Judah shows that those who remain faithful maintain sight, clarity, and discernment.

sens: State of one who cannot see
Spiritual inability to understand or receive divine truth
H5788B.detail:
1. Blindness is the absence of sight, the inability to see: in Leviticus 22:22, a blind animal cannot be offered as a sacrifice to the Lord, for it would have a defect.
2. Blindness can also refer to a spiritual inability to perceive the truth of God, a closing of the mind to the divine message.
H5788B.origine: The Hebrew word עִוָּרוֹן (ivaron, blindness) derives from עָוַר (avar), which means "to be blind." This form עַוֶּרֶת is a variant. The root evokes the idea of not seeing, of lacking light. The word is used to describe both physical condition and, in prophetic or wisdom language, a spiritual condition.
H5788B.emploi: This word appears in Leviticus 22:22 to describe a defect that renders an animal unfit for sacrifice. In Israelite law, an animal intended to be offered to the Lord had to be without defect: blindness, like lameness or disease, marked an imperfection that rendered the beast unworthy of worship. It is a concrete application of the requirement for perfection in the service of the holy God.
H5788B.portee: For the believer, this word serves as a reminder that God demands integrity in the worship rendered to Him. Beyond the animal sacrifice, it invites reflection on spiritual vision: are we blind to the realities of God's kingdom? Let us ask Him to open our eyes to His truth.

sens: To hurry, to rush to go quickly
To accelerate one's action, one's movement
H5789.detail:
1. "Hasten" means to hurry, to go quickly, to rush. It is to move with urgency, without dragging. In Joel 3:11, the call "Hasten and come, you all nations around" invites the nations to gather without delay, pressed as if by an imminent danger or threat.
2. The verb also expresses the acceleration of an action: one hurries to accomplish something as quickly as possible, with eagerness and speed.
H5789.origine: The Hebrew verb עוּשׁ comes from a root that evokes rapid movement and urgency. In Hebrew, words of the same family express the idea of speed and haste. The fundamental meaning is that of a person moving quickly, accelerating their pace— a concrete image of haste.
H5789.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joel 3:11. In this dramatic prophetic context, it calls the nations to gather hastily, without delay. The rarity of the word in Scripture suggests that it has retained a rather poetic and solemn usage, reserved for moments where urgency and haste are strongly emphasized.
H5789.portee: This verb reminds us that some calls from God require an immediate response. To hasten our steps toward God is to recognize the importance of the moment and the urgency of following the Lord, without procrastination or hesitation.

sens: To help someone, to assist them in their weakness or distress
To uplift by words one who is discouraged or afflicted
H5790.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of hastening to someone to provide help, to come to their aid in a moment of need. It is to intervene quickly to support one who is collapsing or suffering.

2. In the usage of Isaiah 50:4, the meaning becomes clearer: it is to support by words, that is, to uplift the heart of one who is downcast. The Servant of the Lord learns to speak with a trained tongue in order to know how to comfort by his words the one who is staggering under the weight of pain. It is a moral and spiritual help, conveyed through fitting and compassionate words.
H5790.origine: The Hebrew root עוּת (ut) expresses the idea of coming forward, of quickly coming to help. The word draws its image from the urgent movement of the rescuer rushing toward one in need. Although the exact form is rare in the Hebrew Bible, it belongs to the semantic field of support and assistance.
H5790.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Isaiah 50:4. It describes the role of the suffering Servant of the Lord: he receives a trained tongue to support by words the one who is downcast. The context reveals that this support is not physical but spiritual and moral: it is the ability to address the right word at the right moment to the one who suffers, restoring hope and strength. This unique usage makes it a word difficult to date precisely, but its prophetic context is clear.
H5790.portee: This verb teaches us that true help is often not material but spiritual: it resides in a fitting word, spoken with compassion to the one who suffers. For the believer, this serves as a reminder of the importance of being attentive to others, to listen as you are taught, and to know how to comfort with the words of consolation that the Spirit puts in our mouths.

sens: Make crooked, twisted, bent
Distort, falsify, misrepresent
Overturn, destroy, annihilate
Circumvent, violate a law or right
H5791.detail:
1. The basic physical meaning: to make something straight twisted or crooked. It is the image of something being bent or curved. Ecclesiastes 1:15 expresses this clearly: "What is crooked cannot be made straight" — it speaks of a physical or moral reality that can no longer be corrected.
2. By extension, to falsify or distort something immaterial: the truth, words, a decision. One twists the meaning of things, making them unrecognizable. Job 8:3 asks: "Would God pervert justice?" — that is, would God change His justice into its opposite?
3. To overturn or annihilate: to destroy the established order, to bring down what was standing. Psalms 146:9 says that the Lord "overturns the way of the wicked" — He destroys their path, their plans.
4. To willfully violate a law or right, to transgress them. Job 34:12 affirms that the Almighty "does not violate justice" — He does not divert it from its purpose.
H5791.origine: The Hebrew word עָוַת (avat) comes from a root that expresses the idea of bending, folding, twisting. It is related to the concrete image of something being made crooked or bent. In Hebrew, this verb first describes a physical action, then extends to moral and legal meanings: to pervert means to twist what is right, particularly justice, truth, or the established order.
H5791.emploi: The verb appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Ecclesiastes, Psalms) and the prophets (Amos, Lamentations). It almost always denotes a bad action or an irreparable situation. In Job (8:3, 34:12), it expresses the impossibility that God would pervert or violate His own justice. In Psalms (146:9) and Lamentations (3:36), it describes how God or the wicked overturn, distort, or destroy what is just. Ecclesiastes uses the word to express absurdity: what is bent by fate or evil cannot be straightened (1:15). The context reveals that to pervert is to distort God's just order, whether voluntarily (through sin) or through the alienated human condition.
H5791.portee: This word highlights the critical importance of justice and righteousness in biblical thought. It reminds the reader that God cannot — and does not — circumvent or falsify His own justice, even to save one who suffers. It also calls the believer not to twist truth or right for convenience. It is a word of moral stability: certain things, once twisted by sin or evil, can only be straightened by God alone.

sens: Action of bending, folding downwards
Diverting justice, perverting right
Injustice inflicted on one who cannot defend themselves
H5792.detail: 1. The word first evokes the physical image of bending or folding something downwards, deforming it — this is the basic idea contained in its root. 2. In moral and legal senses, it denotes the diversion of justice: it is when one "bends" the law, when one perverts right to serve personal interests or to mistreat someone. 3. In Lamentations 3:59, the grieving prophet says to God: "You have seen, Lord, the oppression of which I am a victim" — he speaks of the injustice suffered, of the mistreatment inflicted by those who abuse their power against a weak person who cannot defend themselves.
H5792.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to bend" or "to fold" — hence the image of something being forced to deform. Applied to justice and human relationships, this image of distortion has taken on the meaning of injustice and mistreatment: one "bends" right, one "bends" the weak person under the weight of abusive power.
H5792.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Lamentations 3:59. The context is that of the entire book: Jerusalem has been destroyed by the Babylonians, and the prophet mourns the catastrophe. He acknowledges that God has seen the oppression, the injustice that His people have suffered. This solitary cry shows how this term summarizes the suffering of one who has endured evil without being able to escape it.
H5792.portee: This word reminds us that God sees oppression, that it does not escape His gaze. For the biblical reader, it is a promise: when one suffers injustice, one can cry out to God knowing that He knows our oppression. It is also a call not to ignore injustice, to plead for those who suffer the perversion of right without defense.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the Exile and Return
H5793G.detail: Uthai is a proper name designating two different characters in the Old Testament. The first is a descendant of Perez, son of the tribe of Judah, whose genealogy is given in 1 Chronicles 9:4: he is the son of Ammihud, who is himself the son of Omri. The second Uthai is mentioned in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon with the second caravan of Ezra, and he is listed among the sons of Bigvai. These two mentions show the importance given by the Bible to genealogies and the lists of those who reconstituted the people after the Exile.
H5793G.origine: The name Uthai comes from Hebrew and means "helpful" or "useful," evoking the idea of aid and support. It is a theophoric name that reflects a blessing or a desired quality for the one who bears it.
H5793G.emploi: Uthai appears only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 9:4, in the context of the genealogies of Judah at the time of the return from Exile. This verse presents him as the son of Ammihud and as a member of the tribe of Judah who regained his place in the restored people after the Babylonian captivity. The presence of his name in this genealogical list emphasizes that even ordinary families of the people have a role and a trace in the history of salvation.

sens: Member of the family of Bigvai who returned from exile with Ezra
H5793H.detail: Uthai is a man from the time of the return from exile, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is one of the sons of Bigvai, those families who had been deported to Babylon and who return to Jerusalem under the leadership of Ezra. In Ezra 8:14, he is listed among those who return to the Holy Land with seventy other men from his household.
H5793H.origine: The name Uthai means "useful" or "one who helps." It is a compound Hebrew name that expresses a positive quality. Uthai appears as an ordinary character of the Jewish people, with no other details given about his life or role.
H5793H.emploi: Uthai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:14. He appears in the list of family heads who join the second caravan of return from exile led by the scribe Ezra, probably in the fifth century B.C. His name appears among the descendants of important families of Judah who were exiled to Babylon and who restore the Jewish community in Jerusalem.

sens: One who possesses great physical or military strength
One who manifests violence, brutality, or severity
One who is intense, irresistible, difficult to control
One who has influence, authority, or domination over others
One who is impetuous, carried away by desires or feelings
Boundary, limit (secondary and rare meaning)
H5794.detail:
1. **Powerful in the sense of physical or military strength**: the word refers to one who has great bodily or warrior power. Reuben is presented as superior "in power" (Genesis 49:3), which evokes his physical superiority as the firstborn; the walls of Canaan are described as "powerful" (Numbers 13:28), meaning fortified and formidable.
2. **Violent, brutal, cruel**: the word depicts one who acts harshly or without mercy. The rich responds to the poor "harshly" (Proverbs 18:23), contemptuously; the "cruel" king of Egypt (Isaiah 19:4) reigns by brute force, without clemency.
3. **Intense and irresistible**: that which imposes itself by its own strength, without being able to be restrained. Love is "as strong as death" (Song of Solomon 8:6), impossible to extinguish; the waves become violent under the wind of the Lord (Exodus 14:21).
4. **Endowed with authority or domination**: one who imposes his will. God delivers Israel "from his powerful adversary" (2 Samuel 22:18), stronger and threatening; a "cruel" king will dominate the Egyptians (Isaiah 19:4).
5. **Impulsive, voracious, unrestrained**: that which aspires to satisfaction without measure. The dogs are "voracious," insatiable in their desire (Isaiah 56:11).
6. **Boundary** (rare and derived meaning): fortified limit of a territory. The boundary of the Ammonites was "fortified" (Numbers 21:24), marking the limits of the land.
H5794.origine: The Hebrew root essentially means "to be strong" or "to prevail." It evokes the idea of a strength that imposes itself, that dominates, often with a nuance of aggressiveness or brutality. The word is used for beings (warriors, kings, animals) and abstract realities (forces, wills, feelings) where there is an indomitable or irresistible power.
H5794.emploi: The word "powerful" appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in poetry (Psalms, Proverbs, Song of Solomon), historical narratives (Numbers, 2 Samuel, Ezekiel), and the prophets (Isaiah). It qualifies sometimes a person (Reuben, a king, an adversary), sometimes a thing (a wall, a wind, love). Its meaning varies according to the context: admiration for warrior strength (Genesis 49:3), fear in the face of a nation's violence (Numbers 13:28), moral reproach against hardness or cruelty (Proverbs 18:23; Isaiah 19:4). The word can also describe a quality of God (his power: Genesis 49:3 "my strength") or of his enemies (their threats). Each use emphasizes less brute strength than what it does: it dominates, it crushes, it imposes itself without resistance.
H5794.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that true strength is not in violence or harshness, but in the power of God. The Lord alone is truly powerful and reserves for humans a strength in the service of justice and mercy. Recognizing God's power invites submission to his authority rather than to the cruel or violent masters of this world.

sens: Domestic animal of herds, small ruminant with pointed horns
Kid, young goat or very young goat
Billy goat, male of the goat
Offering or sacrificial victim to God in Israelite worship
Symbolic representation of confessed and expiated sin (scapegoat)
H5795.detail:
1. The goat is a common domestic animal in the Old Testament, raised in herds like the sheep or cow. It provides milk, meat, and hair used in the construction of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:4). Jacob kept goats in Laban's flocks (Genesis 30:32).
2. A kid is a young animal or a young goat, often chosen for an important meal or offering. Jesse sends one to Saul through David (1 Samuel 16:20).
3. The billy goat is the male of the species. It also refers to the whole animal when presented for sacrifice. The laws of worship regularly require goats for offerings (Leviticus 4:23).
4. The goat or billy goat becomes a sacrificial victim in God's system of offerings to Israel. They are offered to atone for the sins of the people or for various festivities (Numbers 28:30).
5. The billy goat is also the symbol of sin borne and removed: on the Day of Atonement, the high priest confesses the sins of Israel on a goat, which is then sent into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:5).
H5795.origine: The Hebrew word עֵז (ez) is very ancient and refers to the domestic animal since the early times of pastoralism. It has no transparent etymology in Hebrew but also exists in Aramaic with the same meaning. The goat was a basic animal in the economy of the ancient Near East, just like the sheep, and Scripture constantly speaks of it as a normal part of the flock.
H5795.emploi: The word appears 74 times in the Old Testament, mainly in pastoral narratives and in the sacrificial code of the Pentateuch. In the Genesis narratives, the goat or billy goat is part of the wealth of the patriarchs (Jacob keeps spotted goats in Laban's flock, Genesis 30:32-35). In Exodus and Leviticus, the word is very frequent because it designates one of the most common victims of sacrificial worship. Goats are offered for sin, communal atonement, or festivals (Leviticus 9:3; Numbers 28:30). Goat hair is also used in the construction of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:4). On the Day of Atonement, the billy goat becomes a living symbol of sin removed (Leviticus 16).
H5795.portee: The goat reminds us that Israel's worship was rooted in ordinary pastoral life: God required animals that the Israelites truly possessed, tied to their livelihood. The sacrifice of the billy goat, especially on the Day of Atonement, teaches that sin had a price, and that something had to die in place of the guilty. This image prepares the reader to understand Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

sens: male goat of the goat, used in sacrifices
victim offered to erase the sins of a community
H5796.detail:
1. The scapegoat is the male of the domestic goat, a common animal in ancient Israel. In temple worship, it was offered as a sacrifice, particularly for the sins of the people.
2. The scapegoat carries a precise religious significance: it is the animal whose spilled blood "covers" transgressions and purifies the sanctuary. In Ezra 6:17, during the dedication of the temple rebuilt after the exile, twelve goats are offered, one for each tribe of Israel, so that forgiveness extends to all the people without exception.
H5796.origine: The Aramaic word עֵז (ez) is related to the Hebrew עֵז (ez, H5795), which simply designates the goat or billy goat. Its initial image is that of the animal itself. In the biblical religious lexicon, the scapegoat takes on a particular sacrificial charge: it is the animal chosen par excellence for expiatory sacrifices, as its blood was considered particularly effective in restoring the relationship between the sinful people and God.
H5796.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic text of Ezra (6:17), during the account of the dedication of the second temple. The context shows that the twelve goats offered in sacrifice had an expiatory function for all the tribes of Israel: each goat represented one of them. This detail emphasizes how God's forgiveness was envisioned as covering the entirety of the restored people.
H5796.portee: This sacrifice of scapegoats reminds the reader that the forgiveness of sins comes through the offering of blood. For the Christian, this image prepares the understanding of the unique sacrifice of Christ, whose blood shed once for all replaces all former sacrifices and purifies his people definitively.

sens: Physical or material power, capacity for movement or resistance
Energy, vigor of a person
Political or military power, authority of a state or leader
Divine power, attribute of God
Support, backing, protection
Glory, honor, splendor
H5797.detail: 1. Strength can be that of a body that moves or resists: it is muscular power or the solidity of a fortification. Job 12:16 states that God "possesses strength," the kind that masters men and things. 2. It is also the vigor and endurance of a living person: Proverbs 31:17 speaks of a woman who "girds her loins with strength." 3. Strength becomes political or military power, the capacity of a people or a king to stand against their enemies and to reign: Isaiah 45:24 asserts that "justice and strength belong to the Lord alone." 4. Above all, it is divine power, the creative and saving arm of God: Exodus 15:2 sings, "The Lord is my strength and the subject of my praise." 5. Strength is also what supports and protects: Psalms 59:18 exclaims, "O my strength! I will sing praises to you," referring to God as a refuge. 6. Finally, it denotes glory and honor: 1 Chronicles 16:27 places "strength and splendor" in the sanctuary of God.
H5797.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of standing up, of standing firm. It is related to other words expressing solidity, hardness, or permanence. In itself, oz paints the image of an energy that settles, that holds firm. It is not a brute and disorderly force, but a controlled power, capable of supporting, protecting, and reigning.
H5797.emploi: The word appears 91 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms (55 occurrences), Proverbs, Isaiah, and Job. It is a fundamental word of praise and prayer: it is used to celebrate the power of God who creates (Psalms 93:1, "the Lord reigns, he is clothed with strength"), who saves (Exodus 15:2), who supports his faithful (Psalms 28:7, "the Lord is my strength and my shield"). But it is also used to describe human power: that of a king, an army, a fortified city, or the vigor of a wise man (Proverbs 24:5). The context shows that strength can be vain if it is not founded on God: that is why the Psalms constantly ask God to "strengthen" or "give strength," recognizing that all true power comes from him.
H5797.portee: This word reminds the believer that true strength is not that of muscles or weapons, but that of God. Recognizing the Lord as one's strength means renouncing reliance on one's own abilities and leaning on his infinite power to face adversity. For a disciple of Jesus, this also means that one's weakness becomes a place where divine strength operates.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Abinadab, brother of Ahio
The one who was struck dead for touching the ark of God
H5798A.detail: Uzzah is a man from the time of the united monarchy, son of Abinadab, who lived in the hilly region. With his brother Ahio, he drives the new cart that carries the ark of God when David decides to bring it back to Jerusalem. Seeing that the oxen stumbled, Uzzah reached out his hand to steady it — a natural and protective gesture. But it is an act of transgression: only the Levitical priests had the right to touch the sacred ark. His profane hand on the most holy object of Israel provokes the anger of God, who strikes him dead on the spot. David, astonished, names the place "Perez-Uzzah" ("breach of Uzzah"), to commemorate the divine judgment.
H5798A.origine: The name Uzzah means "strength" or "power" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes solidity and robustness. It is a name borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, but the most famous episode is that of this son of Abinadab, known precisely for that moment when his human strength presumed to intervene where only divine order could act.
H5798A.emploi: Uzzah appears in two parallel accounts: that of 2 Samuel 6 and that of 1 Chronicles 13. Both recount the same event: the solemn transport of the ark of God and the sudden death of Uzzah for having touched it. This incident marks a turning point in the procession: David understands that the ark can only be transported according to divine prescriptions, and its transport is halted for three months. The name becomes inseparable from this terrible judgment, and the place of the drama forever bears his name.
H5798A.portee: The story of Uzzah teaches the believer that respect for the holiness of God is not a matter of good intentions. Even a well-intentioned gesture, even a desire to serve, does not authorize the violation of divine commandments. It reminds us that access to God is obtained through obedience to the ways he has established, not through our personal initiatives. For the Christian, it also foreshadows the importance of order and purity in worship, and the necessity of respecting the mediation established by God.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Merari, living at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel
H5798B.detail: Uzza is a man belonging to the tribe of Levi, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is also known as "Uzzah." He lived at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms (after the reign of Solomon). His name means "strength" or "power." Uzza is a descendant of Merari (one of the three sons of Levi) and appears in the genealogy of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:29).
H5798B.origine: The name Uzza comes from a root that means "to be strong" or "to have strength." It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a divine quality or trust in God. In the Old Testament, several characters bear this name or a close variant (Uzziah, Azariah), reflecting this same idea of strength and power.
H5798B.emploi: Uzza appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:29. He is included in a long genealogy of the Levites from the branch of Merari. It is a purely genealogical role: he is presented as the son of Shimei and the father of Shimea, in the line of descent of the servants of the Temple.

sens: Garden near Jerusalem where the kings of Judah were buried
H5798G.detail: 1. A garden located in or near Jerusalem, which served as a royal burial place. It is in the garden of Uzza that King Manasseh was buried after his death (2 Kings 21:18), and where his son Amon was also buried (2 Kings 21:26). This garden was probably attached to the royal residence and constituted a private cemetery for the royal family.
H5798G.origine: The name Uzza (עֻזָּא) means "strength" or "power" in Hebrew, derived from a root denoting strength and robustness. It is the same word that forms the proper name Uzzah, a Levite from the family of Merari mentioned elsewhere in Scripture. The garden bears this name, perhaps in honor of a person, owner, or founder.
H5798G.emploi: The garden of Uzza appears twice in the account of the Kings of Judah, only in 2 Kings 21. It is mentioned as the burial place of two kings: Manasseh (v. 18) and his son Amon (v. 26). These two kings, although their reigns brought religious troubles to Judah, received an honorable burial in this royal garden, indicating that it was a necropolis reserved for monarchs and their close family. The garden represents an important element of the royal funeral ritual in Judah.
H5798G.portee: This place reminds us that even kings who strayed from God's ways received a dignified burial, according to the customs of their time. The garden of Uzza symbolizes the permanence of royal and funerary practices in Jerusalem, regardless of religious infidelities. For the Christian, this underscores that earthly honor, including a beautiful burial, is not sufficient if one's life has not honored God.

sens: Son of Ehud, from the tribe of Benjamin, living before the monarchy of Israel
H5798H.detail: Uzza is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Ehud and the brother of Naaman, Ahijah, Gera, and Ahichud. He appears in the genealogy of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8:7, where his name is listed among the descendants of this tribe.
H5798H.origine: The name Uzza means "strength" or "power" in Hebrew. It comes from the root עז (oz) which expresses strength and solidity. This name was borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, reflecting the importance placed on power and solidity among the Hebrews.
H5798H.emploi: Uzza appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:7, where he is mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. This passage lists the sons of Ehud and their descendants, thus establishing the tribal history of Israel before the establishment of the monarchy. His brief mention shows that he was a recognized ancestor of the tribe, even though few details are given about his life or actions.

sens: Man from the period of Exile and Return
Name of a Levitical family
H5798I.detail:
1. Uzza is the name of a man who lived at the time of the Return from the Babylonian Exile, around the mid-fifth century B.C. He is first mentioned in the list of those who returned with Ezra.
2. Uzza is also the name of a family or lineage — referred to as the "sons of Uzza" — that was part of the Levitical people in Jerusalem. This family is listed in the records of the families of priests and temple servants who returned from captivity (Ezra 2:49; Nehemiah 7:51).
H5798I.origine: The name Uzza means "strength" or "power" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses vigor and solidity. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the father's trust in divine strength. The name appears multiple times in biblical genealogies, particularly among the Levites.
H5798I.emploi: Uzza appears twice in Scripture, always in the context of lists of returnees after the Exile. In the book of Ezra (2:49), the families of temple servants who returned from Babylon with Ezra are enumerated, and the family of Uzza is included among them. The same list is repeated with some minor variations in the book of Nehemiah (7:51). These mentions remind us that the people of God, beyond the Exile, had reorganized and restored themselves, with their priests and Levites returned to their place.

sens: The goat on which lots were cast to send it alive into the wilderness, symbolically bearing the sins of the people
The act of sending away the sin-bearing goat
By extension, the total atonement for the sins of the people
H5799.detail:
1. Azazel primarily refers to the goat that the high priest sent alive into the wilderness on the annual Day of Atonement. Lots were cast between two goats: one was offered as a sacrifice to God, the other was designated for Azazel and released to carry away the guilt of the people (Leviticus 16:8, 16:10). This was a dramatic and concrete act, unique in Israel's worship.
2. Azazel can also refer to the action itself: the sending away of the goat, which represented the removal of all confessed sins by Israel (Leviticus 16:26). The man who led the goat into the wilderness had to wash himself and his clothes, marking the reality of the symbolic transfer.
3. Spiritually, Azazel represents complete and definitive atonement: the sins of the people do not remain to accuse them; they are taken away, sent far away. This is why this rite continues to fascinate: it expresses that true forgiveness removes evil forever.
H5799.origine: The etymology of Azazel remains debated. Its literal meaning could be "the goat that departs" or "strong God" (from two Hebrew roots), but the Bible does not explain it itself. This term appears only in the context of the Yom Kippur celebration, the Day of Atonement, suggesting that the word carries the idea of sending away or distancing. No other Hebrew word closely resembles it, and its exact origin remains a mystery that scholars have discussed since antiquity.
H5799.emploi: Azazel appears only three times in the Bible, all in Leviticus 16, at the heart of the high priest's ritual on the Day of Atonement. In Leviticus 16:8, the two goats are chosen by lot: one for the Lord, the other for Azazel. In Leviticus 16:10, the goat designated for Azazel is presented alive to make atonement. In Leviticus 16:26, the man who leads the goat must wash. Everything revolves around this unique gesture: two goats, one lot, two different destinies that together symbolized the complete restoration of the people's relationship with God.
H5799.portee: This ritual of the goat for Azazel speaks to the heart of the Christian: it shows that God, even in the Old Testament, wanted sins to be truly removed, not simply covered. The goat that flees into the wilderness foreshadows Christ who bore our sins outside the city and cast them far from us (Hebrews 13:11-12). It is a promise: forgiven sins do not return to accuse us.
